# Class compilation and library reuse

Zero parses TypeScript with OXC 0.152.0, evaluates configuration as pure data,
and compiles saved callbacks to PHP. Classes participate in that same pipeline.
The [authoring reference](config-api.md#classes-in-callbacks) defines the supported
surface and refusals. This is a bounded TypeScript backend, not an npm executor.

## Representation and initialization

`src/compile/classes.rs` emits descriptor factories and ordinary PHP functions
with explicit receivers. `runtime/Zero/JsClass.php` supplies dispatch and ancestry;
instances remain the existing `JsObject` handles. Field storage, aliasing,
closures, object enumeration and JSON therefore use the existing runtime owners.
Descriptors live outside enumerable own fields. Parent dispatch keeps the actual
receiver, while `super` starts lookup at the lexical parent.

Base fields run before constructor defaults. Derived fields run after the first
`super(...)`, including through an omitted forwarding constructor. Parameter
properties follow TypeScript's ES2022 field emit: their fields exist before
ordinary field initializers and receive argument values before the authored
constructor body. Early field reads include null. Calling methods or allowing
instances to escape during initialization is refused, keeping inference away
from partially initialized virtual receivers.

`src/compile/effects.rs` remains the mutation-analysis owner. Constructors,
initializers and methods become call edges; receiver arguments participate in
existing alias, capture and read-invalidation analysis. The class instance type
keeps nominal ancestry and an own-field shape. Wire/client types, clones and
persisted snapshots erase that ancestry. JSON schemas cannot claim to hydrate
an instance.

it preserves the current parser and source locations. Class emission stays on
Zero's typed IR in this change, retaining annotations and the existing value
model. A library migration needs a measured benefit beyond additional syntax;
SWC does not currently remove a PHP-specific obligation that justifies that cost.
Broader TypeScript support should add behavior to the existing owners and run
Node/generated-PHP comparisons before widening accepted syntax.

`tests/compiler_contracts.rs` owns class compilation, source-located refusals,
JSON/Seam detachment and strict generated-client checks. Its differential case
uses `tests/differential/classes.ts`, TypeScript's ES2022 emit, the existing Node
oracle, and the actual generated PHP loaded with the emitted runtime. It compares
complete action results, including constructor order, inherited/overridden

implementation source text.

The shared PHP suite continues to own object/array and WordPress boundary
behavior. Class evidence adds descriptor-specific behavior at the compiler seam;

# Compiler diagnostics

`zero check [project-dir] --json` compiles in memory and writes one JSON object
to stdout. It writes no generated files, migrations or plugin downloads. Exit
status is 0 for a successful check, 1 for a compiler diagnostic, and 2 for invalid
CLI arguments. Argument errors remain human-readable on stderr.

```sh
zero check examples/recipes --json
python3 scripts/compiler-contracts.py --check
```

The website's browser build of the compiler (`src/wasm.rs`) answers with the same
envelope under `check`, so an editor, the command line and the site report one shape.

The envelope has `schema: "zero-diagnostics"`, `version: 1`, `compilerVersion`,
`ok`, `diagnostics` and `groups`. Both arrays are empty on success. Each
diagnostic has a code, category, severity, message, optional help, location and
group ID. Categories currently are `invalid-source`, `unsupported` and
`environment`; severity currently is `error`.

A location contains a project-relative file path where possible, zero-based
UTF-8 byte `start` and exclusive `end` offsets, and one-based `line`, `column`,
`endLine` and `endColumn` positions. Columns count UTF-16 code units for editor
integration. The envelope declares `offsetEncoding: "utf-8"` and
`positionEncoding: "utf-16"`. A diagnostic without a source location has
`location: null`. This encoding describes diagnostics, independently of runtime
string indexing.

Groups collect identical codes and messages with distinct source locations.
Their IDs are opaque hashes of the code/message; do not infer a diagnostic code
from the ID. IDs are independent of the project directory. Message changes can
change a group ID. Sites and groups retain deterministic module traversal order.
Repeated instantiation messages with different text are currently separate groups.

Parsing/lowering collects independent failures in top-level declarations and
imported modules. A failed declaration is discarded only for continued analysis;
if any failure occurred, the entire program is rejected before evaluation. No
partially lowered config or executable artifact is produced. A syntax failure
prevents lowering that module, while other imports already discovered in valid
modules can still be checked. Evaluation, extraction and PHP type checking still
stop at their first error. This is not a complete tolerant TypeScript checker.

The ordinary `zero check` keeps its terminal output and first-error behavior.
The JSON form also fails on unsupported constructs; a report containing blockers
never exits successfully. It checks the WordPress compilation contract without requiring target flags. Nonfatal build hints are not currently included in the JSON
format.

## Codes

- `Z0001`: general configuration error.
- `Z1001`: TypeScript syntax error.
- `Z1002`: unsupported syntax/lowering operation.
- `Z1003`: module/file resolution or read failure.
- `Z2001`: pure evaluation failure.
- `Z3001`: schema extraction failure.
- `Z4001`: handler type checking or PHP compilation failure.

Specific, fixture-backed codes take precedence over phase codes. The growing
[tested compatibility inventory](language-support.md) lists those codes and
guidance. Add the diagnostic at its source, a rejection fixture and an inventory
entry together. Run `python3 scripts/compiler-contracts.py` after changing the
inventory; `cargo test --test compiler_contracts` verifies actual CLI outcomes
and rejects stale generated documentation.

# zero.config.ts API (v0) `zero build` reads `zero.config.ts`, evaluates it at build time with Zero's own Rust evaluator (no Node, no JS engine), and compiles hooks/actions to PHP. Everything below is exported from the `"zero"` module. Shapes follow Drizzle ORM 1.0 (beta.22): column builders, `defineRelations`, relational-query `findMany`/`findFirst` with object filters. ## WordPress plugins Use a top-level package map in `defineConfig`: ```ts plugins: { "classic-editor": "1.6.7" } ``` Values are exact WordPress.org versions or resource objects with `version`, `pluginData`, optional `requires`, and a checksum (required for direct URLs). See [plugin dependencies](wp-plugins.md) for resources, locks and assembly. ## Mixed content and app data ```ts import { collection, table, text, integer, defineRelations, defineConfig, } from "zero"; // Native WordPress content with an editor and an implicit id: id(). const posts = collection({ title: text().notNull() }); // App data in SQL, with a reference to the content. const stock = table({ postId: integer().references(() => posts.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }), quantity: integer().notNull().default(0), }); const collections = { posts }; const tables = { stock }; const relations = defineRelations({ ...collections, ...tables }, (r) => ({ stock: { post: r.one.posts({ from: r.stock.postId, to: r.posts.id }) }, posts: { stock: r.many.stock() }, })); export default defineConfig({ collections, tables, relations, hooks: { posts: { beforeCreate(data) { data.title = data.title.trim(); } } }, }); ``` The generated client stays flat: `zero.posts.create({ title: "Hello" })`, `zero.stock.create({ postId, quantity: 2 })`, then `zero.stock.list({ where: { post: { title: "Hello" } }, with: { post: true } })`. See the [pantry](../examples/pantry/zero.config.ts) for a table-only app and [blog](../examples/blog/zero.config.ts) for editorial content with related app data. ## Columns The SQL column is the one a `table()` gets in the generated MySQL migration; a `collection()` stores the same values as post fields and meta. | builder | SQL | TS select type | |---|---|---| | `id()` | BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT, primary key | `number` | | `integer()` | BIGINT | `number` | | `real()` | DOUBLE | `number` | | `text()` / `text({ enum: [...] })` | LONGTEXT (VARCHAR when unique, when `.max()` is 191 or less, or for an enum) | `string` / union of the enum | | `boolean()` | TINYINT(1) 0/1 | `boolean` | | `timestamp()` | CHAR(24) (UTC ISO-8601 with ms); writes take epoch ms or ISO 8601 with `Z`/`±HH:MM` (a bare `YYYY-MM-DD` is UTC midnight) | `string` | | `date()` | CHAR(10) `YYYY-MM-DD`, a real calendar day | `string` | | `json()` / `json().$type()` | LONGTEXT (JSON; an object keyed exactly `"0"`, `"1"`, ... reads back as a list, so a `.default()` can't contain one) | `unknown` / `T` | | `text({ multiline: true })` | LONGTEXT | `string` (textarea in wp-admin) | | `email()` / `url()` | VARCHAR or LONGTEXT as `text()`, validated | `string` | | `slug({ source? })` | VARCHAR(200), unique, `^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$`, derived from `source` when omitted | `string` | | `richText()` | LONGTEXT (HTML) | `string` | | `media({ accept? })` | BIGINT media id | `number` (a media row with `with: { col: true }`) | | `media({ multiple: true })` | LONGTEXT (JSON ids) | `number[]` | | `select({ options })` | same as `text({ enum })` | union of the options | | `select({ options, multiple: true })` | LONGTEXT (JSON) | `option[]` | | `group({ fields })` | LONGTEXT (JSON) | `{ ...fields }` | | `repeater({ fields })` | LONGTEXT (JSON) | `{ ...fields }[]` | | `blocks({ layouts })` | LONGTEXT (JSON) | `({ layout: "a", ...a } \| { layout: "b", ...b })[]` | Modifiers (each returns a new builder; builders are immutable so shared field sets are safe): `.notNull()`, `.default(value)`, `.defaultNow()` (timestamp/date), `.$default(() => value)` / `.$defaultFn(...)` (runs in PHP on insert), `.$onUpdate(() => value)` / `.$onUpdateFn(...)` (runs in PHP on update; `() => new Date()` on a timestamp is recognized as "now"), `.unique()`, `.primaryKey()`, `.references(() => other.col, { onDelete, onUpdate })` with actions `"cascade" | "restrict" | "set null" | "no action"`, `.$type()` (type only), `.min(n)` / `.max(n)` (numbers: bounds; strings: length; lists: item count), `.pattern(/re/)` (strings), `.validate((value, ctx) => true | "message")` (compiled to PHP, runs on every write). A hidden field is absent from the row (not `null`), and filtering or ordering by it is refused (403). Omitted operations follow the collection. On WordPress it holds in wp-admin and core `/wp/v2` too (see [Access](#access)). - `.ui({ label?, help?, placeholder?, width? })`: presentation metadata. Text properties are strings; width is an integer percentage from 1 to 100. A call replaces the whole UI descriptor, and returns a new builder. Native SCF uses label, plain-text help, width and placeholders on supported input controls; schema description preserves metadata for other consumers. Scalar siblings, ANDed, with a top-level `OR`. It never hides data from the API. - `.localized()`: the field is translated per locale (text, richText, json, select, group, repeater, blocks). Fields never choose storage. Register each definition in its matching namespace: ```ts const posts = collection({ title: text().notNull() }); const stock = table({ postId: integer().references(() => posts.id) }); export default defineConfig({ collections: { posts }, tables: { stock } }); ``` Definitions need no exports. Backend-only config is sufficient; `zero build` emits `zero.gen.ts` to type `db.query` without importing authored definitions. An `id: id()` primary key is implicit. Tables may declare a custom single primary key; collections and user projections use the native integer `id`. The registry key is the logical name, used verbatim by `db.query`, hooks, relations and the flat generated client (`zero.shoppingList`). Physical names and REST paths default to deterministic snake_case: `shoppingList` → `shopping_list`, `HTTPLogs` → `http_logs`. A table uses `wp_zero_shopping_list`; a collection registers `zero_shopping_list`. Duplicate logical or physical names across all registries are rejected before artifacts are emitted. A definition may be registered once. | option | default | meaning | |---|---|---| | `storageName` | registry key in snake_case | explicit physical resource name without `wp_` / `zero_` prefixes; retain existing storage on upgrade | | `label` | title-cased physical name | wp-admin menus, client docs | | `drafts` | `true` for collections, `false` for tables | adds `status` and `publishedAt`; collections always have native drafts | | `revisions` | `true` for collections, `false` for tables | collections always keep native revisions; tables may opt in | | `title` | a `title: text()` column | WordPress post title; must be `text().notNull()` for collections | | `content` | a `content: richText()` column | WordPress post content | | `access` | read `"anyone"`, writes `"editor"` | see below | | `api` | all `true` | `{ list?, get?, create?, update?, delete? }` | | `uid` | `false` (`true` with `sync`) | stable immutable `uid` on every row | | `sync` | none | project-relative `*.md` or `*.json` pattern for `zero sync` | | `agents` | `true` | expose operations as WordPress abilities | Collections need a title and physical names of at most 15 characters (WordPress prefixes `zero_`). Built-in route names are reserved. User projections retain WordPress identity storage; see [Sign-in](#sign-in). ### Upgrading authoring Replace named builders with unnamed `collection()` or `table()` and register under `collections` or `tables`. Keep the logical keys, existing physical storage and committed migration snapshots. The snapshot format and runtime storage model are unchanged: an authoring-only change must produce no migration. For a persisted name that differs from the derived snake_case name, set `storageName` to the exact name in `zero/migrations/snapshot.json`. For example, old `collection("stockItems", fields, { editor: false, revisions: true })` becomes: ```ts const stockItems = table(fields, { storageName: "stockItems", revisions: true }); export default defineConfig({ name: "my-app", tables: { stockItems } }); ``` Keep the app `name`, logical keys, fields, relations, access and storage options (including drafts, revisions, uid and sync) as before. Bind each resource whose physical name differs, including reference targets. `storageName` accepts letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter; reserved names, duplicate logical keys, duplicate physical names and collection post-type limits still apply. The binding is permanent config, not a one-time rename instruction: retain it on subsequent builds. It controls SQL tables, post types, routes and persisted revision ownership; relations and client properties still use logical keys. 1. Keep the entire committed `zero/migrations/` directory, including the v2 `snapshot.json` and every numbered SQL file. Do not remove registrations as an intermediate step: that authors a destructive migration. 2. Change the builders/registries and add the physical bindings, then run `zero build .`. This authoring-only transition must leave the snapshot and historical SQL unchanged and produce no new numbered SQL. Review with `git diff -- zero/migrations` before deployment. 3. Deploy the generated `.zero/wp-content` plugins together as an ordinary file-copy update to the existing site. The runtime keeps the app's migration ledger, rows, reference targets and revision identities; it has no data migration to apply. Verify existing reads, relations and revision history through the new client/runtime before making schema changes. This also supports old logical aliases: use the original physical name as the binding even if the registry key is different. Changing a binding does not move or rename data. Snapshots contain physical names without old logical aliases. A build that removes existing storage while adding new storage is refused as an ambiguous replacement, even when both names are snake_case. Retain the binding during the authoring cut; stage intentional resource removal separately after reviewing its data migration. ### Access `access: { read, create, update, delete }`, each one of `true`/`false`, `"anyone"`, `"authenticated"` (signed in, guests included), a role (`"guest" < "subscriber" < "author" < "editor" < "admin"`, that role or higher), `"self"` (on a user projection: the signed-in user's own row), or `(ctx) => boolean | filter` with `ctx = { user, op, data? }`. Functions are compiled to PHP like hooks; they can't use `db`. A returned filter is checked against the collection like any literal filter and is ANDed into reads, updates and deletes; create rules return a boolean. Actions take `access` too (default `"editor"`). On WordPress these rules are the only gate, on every path into the data: Zero's API, core `/wp/v2`, wp-admin (lists, the editor, quick edit, revisions, autosaves, search) and abilities. A post type's capabilities (`edit_zero_posts`, `edit_others_zero_posts`, ...) are answered from its rules through `map_meta_cap`, and no role is granted them, so granting one by hand changes nothing. Core reads apply the read rule and field access; core writes and editor saves apply the create, update and field rules, and are authorized on the saved data before they commit. ## Globals `global(name, fields, { label?, access?: { read?, update? } })`, registered in `defineConfig({ globals: { name } })`. Media and private file references work on both kinds. ## Hooks `hooks.` in `defineConfig`: | hook | arguments | notes | |---|---|---| | `beforeCreate` | `(data: Insert, ctx)` | mutate `data` or return a replacement | | `afterCreate` | `(row: Row, ctx)` | | | `beforeUpdate` | `(patch: Partial, existing: Row, ctx)` | mutate `patch` or return a replacement | | `afterUpdate` | `(row: Row, previous: Row, ctx)` | | | `beforeDelete` / `afterDelete` | `(row: Row, ctx)` | throw to abort | `ctx` is `{ user: { id, name, role } | null }`. Throwing anything aborts the request and rolls back every write in it. `throw new HttpError(status, code, message)` picks the HTTP response. ## Actions `action({ input: { ...columns }, access?, handler(input, ctx) { ... } })` → `POST /wp-json/zero/v1/actions/`. `input` uses column builders for validation; the return value is the response `data`. - `idempotent: true`: a request with an `Idempotency-Key` header runs once per key and caller; a repeat returns the stored result, and the same key with different input is a 409. `once(key, fn)` does the same inside any handler. - `signature: { secret: env("NAME"), header, scheme: "zero" | "hmac-sha256" }`: an inbound webhook. A handler that throws is retried with backoff up to `retries`, then marked dead; `ctx.attempt` and `ctx.jobId` say which run this is. Each job is handed to Action Scheduler (cron, or `wp action-scheduler run`); `wp zero jobs list|retry|cancel` manage the queue. A webhook POSTs `{ id, event, collection, at, data: { row, previous? } }` for each matching write (`.created|updated|deleted`, or `"*"`), signed in the `zero-signature` header as `t=,v1=hex(HMAC-SHA256(secret, "t.body"))`. S3 never falls back to durable local storage. It projects existing WordPress users and usermeta, preserving their IDs and authentication; it creates no second user table or post type. It needs `email: email().notNull().unique()`, gets a write-only `password` and an admin-only `role`, and cannot have drafts, revisions, slugs or localization. Both sides may change; it merges per field, and writes `.zero/conflicts/.md` when the same field changed on both (`zero sync resolve ` applies your edit of it). `--check` exits 2 when anything would change. The first sync with a site matches records and deletes nothing. References to a `uid` collection are written as that row's uid. When required references form a cycle that no order of writes can satisfy, sync reports it and writes nothing. ## Database API (hooks and actions only) ```ts await db.query.items.findMany({ where, orderBy, limit, offset, columns, with }); await db.query.items.findFirst({ where, ... }); await db.insert(items).values(row | rows).returning?(); await db.update(items).set(patch).where(filter).returning?(); await db.delete(items).where(filter).returning?(); ``` `where` is the Drizzle 1.0 object filter: `{ col: value }`, `{ col: { eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, notIn, like, ilike, notLike, notIlike, isNull, isNotNull, OR, AND, NOT } }`, top-level `OR`/`AND`/`NOT`, relation keys (`{ location: { kind: "fridge" } }` or `{ location: true }`). `orderBy` is `{ col: "asc" | "desc" }`. These are build errors with the same message the runtime returns. `with: { cover: true }` on a media column puts the media row in place of the id. `await` on these calls compiles to plain blocking PHP calls. ## Known gaps What the design specifies and this build doesn't do yet: - `zero sync --watch` isn't available; run `zero sync` again, or from a scheduler. - Sync skips the columns listed under [Sync](#sync); edit those through the site. ## The subset (enforced at build time) Supported: `const`/`let`, functions, arrows, closures, destructuring, spread, template literals, `if`/`for`/`for...of`/`while`/`switch`/`try`, `?.`, `??`, objects, arrays, type annotations, type aliases, interfaces, generics (erased), `structuredClone`. `encodeURI(value)` and `encodeURIComponent(value)` accept exactly one string in configuration evaluation and compiled handlers. General JS argument coercion and decoding globals are not implemented. Use [`zero check --json`](compiler-diagnostics.md) for machine-readable blockers. The [tested compatibility inventory](language-support.md) links specific restrictions and intentional differences to executable evidence. Indexed array/tuple reads and destructured elements include `null` when an entry is missing (Zero represents `undefined` as PHP null). Check the fetched value or supply a default with `??` or a destructuring initializer. A non-null assertion (`values[0]!`) is available when your code guarantees the entry exists. Objects and arrays have reference identity: assignment, argument passing, spreads and closures share their descendants as in JavaScript. Use `structuredClone(value)` for an independent graph; shared descendants and cycles survive cloning. Class instances become plain own-field objects when cloned. Captured module-level objects live for the PHP process (one web request, or the worker's lifetime), as module data does in Node. Arrays are dense. Writing at `length` appends; writing past `length`, at a negative or fractional index, or at `NaN`/`Infinity` throws `RangeError`. Grow arrays with `push` or `Array.from({ length: n }, mapper)`. Fixed-length callback walks (`map`, `filter`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `reduce`, `flatMap`, `find*`) throw `RangeError` if they reach an index their callback removed. Shrinkage after the final visit or an early return is fine; growth is ignored by these walks. `for…of` and `Array.from(array, mapper)` read live length. Elisions, `new Array(n)`, `delete a[i]`, `a.length = n` and non-numeric index types are compile errors. Zero represents `undefined` as `null`: `typeof undefined` gives `"object"`, `JSON.stringify({ x: undefined })` gives `{"x":null}`, `String(undefined)` gives `"null"`, and destructuring defaults also fire on explicit `null`. Optional parameters include null in body reads; defaults supply missing values. Build-time evaluation forbids I/O, `Date.now()`, `new Date()`, `Math.random()`, and `db`, and stops runaway loops with a step budget. Imports: type-only imports (erased), relative `.ts` files (compiled with the config), and `"zero"`. npm packages are rejected unless they ship TypeScript source that fits the subset (not implemented yet: today they're rejected). ### Classes in callbacks Declare concrete named classes at module scope, including in relative modules with named exports. Construct them inside actions, hooks and other compiled callbacks. Public instance fields, ordinary methods, `this` member reads and writes, `new`, identity comparisons, named `extends`, overrides, `super(...)`, `super.method(...)` and `instanceof` are supported. Arrows inside methods keep that method's `this`. `typeof Counter` returns `"function"`; instances return `"object"`. Extracting a prototype method is refused; use `() => instance.method()` when passing a callback. ```ts class Counter { value = 0; constructor(public label: string) {} add(n: number): number { this.value += n; return this.value; } reader(): () => number { return () => this.value; } } class DoubleCounter extends Counter { add(n: number): number { return super.add(n * 2); } } const countVisits = action({ input: {}, handler: () => { const counter = new DoubleCounter("visits"); const read = counter.reader(); counter.add(2); return { value: read(), isCounter: counter instanceof Counter }; // 4, true }, }); ``` Base fields initialize in declaration order before constructor parameter defaults. Derived fields initialize immediately after `super(...)`, before the rest of the constructor. A derived constructor must call `super(...)` as its first statement; an omitted constructor forwards arguments to the parent. Public/readonly typed TypeScript parameter properties create own fields, then receive their parameter values before authored constructor statements. Defaults and other field initializers cannot read those parameter values yet, matching TypeScript's ES2022 class-field emit. Uninitialized fields read as nullable because missing/undefined is PHP null. Field types infer from plain data initializers; annotate fields initialized from `this` or calls. Parameters need a type or a primitive default. Annotate recursive, forward or overridden method returns when inference cannot establish a signature. Derived instances can pass to helpers expecting their base. Mutation effects include receivers, arguments, constructors, inherited methods and captured values; numeric updates widen literal reads and writes invalidate prior narrowing. Static fields start from pure build-time data and live for the PHP process. Static methods inherit and dispatch with the actual class receiver. A subclass write to an inherited static field creates its own value; nested objects retain their shared identity. Static initializers cannot use runtime `this`, construct instances or perform I/O. Instances retain identity through assignment, arguments and closures. JSON responses and generated client types contain own fields only; they do not include methods or class metadata. Object spread copies own fields shallowly. `structuredClone`, stored JSON, callback inputs and persistent `once` results produce plain data without class identity. Use object types in `json().$type()`; class types and assertions that would pretend to hydrate a class are refused. These class features remain outside the supported surface, with located errors: class expressions, default-export class declarations and anonymous/local/abstract/ambient/generic classes; decorators; private/protected/`#` members; accessors; static blocks; computed names; generic/rest methods; dynamic or built-in inheritance; constructor return values; prototype/reflection machinery and custom coercion/serialization protocol members. Indexed class members and recursive class field types are also refused. Uninitialized optional fields follow the same missing-to-null boundary. Class values are limited to construction, `instanceof`, `typeof` and static access. Method calls and escaping instances during construction/initialization are refused to avoid partially initialized virtual receivers. Construction and method calls inside access rules are refused; return filters from plain functions instead. See [class compilation and library reuse](class-compilation.md) for the runtime representation, validation owners and the OXC/SWC assessment. This support does not enable arbitrary npm execution.

zero.config.ts API (v0)

zero build reads zero.config.ts, evaluates it at build time with Zero’s own Rust evaluator (no Node, no JS engine), and compiles hooks/actions to PHP. Everything below is exported from the "zero" module. Shapes follow Drizzle ORM 1.0 (beta.22): column builders, defineRelations, relational-query findMany/findFirst with object filters.

WordPress plugins

Use a top-level package map in defineConfig:

plugins: { "classic-editor": "1.6.7" }

Values are exact WordPress.org versions or resource objects with version, pluginData, optional requires, and a checksum (required for direct URLs). See plugin dependencies for resources, locks and assembly.

Mixed content and app data

import {
  collection, table, text, integer, defineRelations, defineConfig,
} from "zero";

// Native WordPress content with an editor and an implicit id: id().
const posts = collection({ title: text().notNull() });
// App data in SQL, with a reference to the content.
const stock = table({
  postId: integer().references(() => posts.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
  quantity: integer().notNull().default(0),
});
const collections = { posts };
const tables = { stock };
const relations = defineRelations({ ...collections, ...tables }, (r) => ({
  stock: { post: r.one.posts({ from: r.stock.postId, to: r.posts.id }) },
  posts: { stock: r.many.stock() },
}));

export default defineConfig({
  collections, tables, relations,
  hooks: { posts: { beforeCreate(data) { data.title = data.title.trim(); } } },
});

The generated client stays flat: zero.posts.create({ title: "Hello" }), zero.stock.create({ postId, quantity: 2 }), then zero.stock.list({ where: { post: { title: "Hello" } }, with: { post: true } }). See the pantry for a table-only app and blog for editorial content with related app data.

Collections, tables and user projections

collection(fields, options?) is editorial content: a WordPress custom post type with the native editor, draft status and revisions. table(fields, options?) is app/relational data in its own SQL table. Fields never choose storage. Register each definition in its matching namespace:

const posts = collection({ title: text().notNull() });
const stock = table({ postId: integer().references(() => posts.id) });
export default defineConfig({ collections: { posts }, tables: { stock } });

Definitions need no exports. Backend-only config is sufficient; zero build emits zero.gen.ts to type db.query without importing authored definitions. An id: id() primary key is implicit. Tables may declare a custom single primary key; collections and user projections use the native integer id.

The registry key is the logical name, used verbatim by db.query, hooks, relations and the flat generated client (zero.shoppingList). Upgrading authoring

Replace named builders with unnamed collection() or table() and register under collections or tables. Keep the logical keys, existing physical storage and committed migration snapshots. The snapshot format and runtime storage model are unchanged: an authoring-only change must produce no migration. For a persisted name that differs from the derived snake_case name, set storageName to the exact name in zero/migrations/snapshot.json. For example, old collection("stockItems", fields, { editor: false, revisions: true }) becomes:

const stockItems = table(fields, { storageName: "stockItems", revisions: true });
export default defineConfig({ name: "my-app", tables: { stockItems } });

Keep the app name, logical keys, fields, relations, access and storage options (including drafts, revisions, uid and sync) as before. Bind each resource whose physical name differs, including reference targets. storageName accepts letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter; reserved names, duplicate logical keys, duplicate physical names and collection post-type limits still apply. The binding is permanent config, not a one-time rename instruction: retain it on subsequent builds. It controls SQL tables, post types, routes and persisted revision ownership; relations and client properties still use logical keys.

  1. Keep the entire committed zero/migrations/ directory, including the v2 snapshot.json and every numbered SQL file. Do not remove registrations as an intermediate step: that authors a destructive migration.
  2. Change the builders/registries and add the physical bindings, then run zero build .. This authoring-only transition must leave the snapshot and historical SQL unchanged and produce no new numbered SQL. Review with git diff -- zero/migrations before deployment.
  3. Deploy the generated .zero/wp-content plugins together as an ordinary file-copy update to the existing site. The runtime keeps the app’s migration ledger, rows, reference targets and revision identities; it has no data migration to apply. Verify existing reads, relations and revision history through the new client/runtime before making schema changes.

This also supports old logical aliases: use the original physical name as the binding even if the registry key is different. Changing a binding does not move or rename data. Snapshots contain physical names without old logical aliases. A build that removes existing storage while adding new storage is refused as an ambiguous replacement, even when both names are snake_case. Retain the binding during the authoring cut; stage intentional resource removal separately after reviewing its data migration.

Access

access: { read, create, update, delete }, each one of true/false, "anyone", "authenticated" (signed in, guests included), a role ("guest" < "subscriber" < "author" < "editor" < "admin", that role or higher), "self" (on a user projection: the signed-in user’s own row), or (ctx) => boolean | filter with ctx = { user, op, data? }. Functions are compiled to PHP like hooks; they can’t use db. A returned filter is checked against the collection like any literal filter and is ANDed into reads, updates and deletes; create rules return a boolean. Actions take access too (default "editor").

On WordPress these rules are the only gate, on every path into the data: Zero’s API, core /wp/v2, wp-admin (lists, the editor, quick edit, revisions, autosaves, search) and abilities. A post type’s capabilities (edit_zero_posts, edit_others_zero_posts, …) are answered from its rules through map_meta_cap, and no role is granted them, so granting one by hand changes nothing. Core reads apply the read rule and field access; core writes and editor saves apply the create, update and field rules, and are authorized on the saved data before they commit.

  • agents: false keeps it out of MCP and the abilities’ public REST discovery; it stays callable over the app’s own API.

Jobs and webhooks

jobs: {
  notifyEditors: job({ input: { commentId: integer().notNull() }, retries: 3, handler: async (input, ctx) => { ... } }),
},
webhooks: [{ url: env("HOOK_URL"), secret: env("HOOK_SECRET"), events: ["posts.created", "posts.updated"] }],

jobs.<name>.enqueue(input, { delay?, key? }) from a hook or action queues a job; it runs after the request commits, never inside it. key collapses duplicates still waiting. A handler that throws is retried with backoff up to retries, then marked dead; ctx.attempt and ctx.jobId say which run this is. Each job is handed to Action Scheduler (cron, or wp action-scheduler run); wp zero jobs list|retry|cancel manage the queue.

A webhook POSTs { id, event, collection, at, data: { row, previous? } } for each matching write (<collection>.created|updated|deleted, or "*"), signed in the zero-signature header as t=<unix>,v1=hex(HMAC-SHA256(secret, "t.body")). Deliveries are jobs, so a failing endpoint is retried. env(name) reads the process environment first, then a wp-config.php constant of that name.

Media and files

media: { sizes: { card: { width: 600, height: 400, fit: "cover" } } } makes each named size for every uploaded image. cover crops around the image’s focal point (PATCH /media/<id> with { focal: { x, y } }, editors only; centre by default); inside scales to fit. Media rows carry sizes.<name>.url.

Private files live in logical file resources:

files: { decks: files("decks", { accept: ["application/pdf"], maxBytes: 20_000_000, access: { read: "owner", delete: "editor" } }) },

and a file({ bucket: "decks" }) column holds one by id. Files never get a public URL: GET /files/<bucket>/<id> returns the row with a signed url valid for five minutes, and that link streams the bytes through PHP. "owner" means the uploader. Uploads outside accept are refused (422 at /file); uploads over maxBytes get 413 payload_too_large.

Configure durable uploads once for the app:

uploads: {
  backend: "s3",
  bucket: env("UPLOAD_BUCKET"),
  region: "us-east-1",
  // endpoint: env("UPLOAD_ENDPOINT"), pathStyle: true, // compatible providers
  prefix: "my-app",
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId: env("UPLOAD_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
    secretAccessKey: env("UPLOAD_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
  },
},

This backend stores private files, media originals and generated sizes, including standard WordPress editor uploads. client.files.decks and file({ bucket: "decks" }) keep naming the logical resource; uploads.bucket is the physical provider bucket. Collections and tables can both reference files and media. Credentials resolve only at runtime; the compiler requires env() references. An optional sessionToken: env("UPLOAD_SESSION_TOKEN") supports temporary credentials.

uploads: { backend: "local" } selects the existing local development behavior (also the default when omitted). S3 never falls back to durable local storage. See upload storage for provider permissions, failure recovery, existing-data cutover and the WordPress plugin boundary.

Locales

locales: { default: "en", all: ["en", "de"] },   // fallback: true by default

A collection with a .localized() field stores one row per locale. Every other field is shared by a post’s translations and kept equal across them, except what each row generates for itself: status, publishedAt, slug, uid, and columns filled by defaultNow(), $default(...) or $onUpdate(...) (so createdAt/updatedAt are per translation). Each translation publishes on its own. Create a translation with { locale: "de", translationOf: <id> }; rows carry locale and translations (locale → id). Reads take ?locale=de, which returns German rows and, with fallback, the default-locale row of any group without one; locale=* returns every row. On WordPress, Polylang owns languages and translation groups, and the app plugin ships a wpml-config.xml saying which fields translate.

Sign-in

Register one userProjection(fields, options?) under users: { members }. It projects existing WordPress users and usermeta, preserving their IDs and authentication; it creates no second user table or post type. It needs email: email().notNull().unique(), gets a write-only password and an admin-only role, and cannot have drafts, revisions, slugs or localization. Members sign in through the typed client: auth.signIn() and auth.handleCallback() redirect through the zero-identity screens (register the frontend once with wp zero-identity app add --name=<name> --id=<app_id> --redirect=<url> --origin=<origin>). GET /me returns the user with their member row.

Anonymous visitors can write as guests (createClient({ auth: { guests: true } })): the first rejected write starts a guest session, and auth.upgrade() keeps the guest’s rows when they sign up.

Sync

{ sync: "content/posts/*.md" }

zero sync --site <url> --app-password user:pass (or --bearer <jwt>) keeps content/posts/<slug>.md and the site in step: front matter for fields, the body as Markdown for the content column. Both sides may change; it merges per field, and writes .zero/conflicts/<uid>.md when the same field changed on both (zero sync resolve <uid> applies your edit of it). --check exits 2 when anything would change. The first sync with a site matches records and deletes nothing. It commits the files it wrote unless --no-commit. zero build adds .zero/* and !.zero/sync-base.json to .gitignore, because the sync base is committed.

What sync leaves out: $onUpdate columns, derived and hidden system columns, and fields the viewer’s field access hides. A synced collection needs id() as its primary key. References to a uid collection are written as that row’s uid. When required references form a cycle that no order of writes can satisfy, sync reports it and writes nothing.

Database API (hooks and actions only)

await db.query.items.findMany({ where, orderBy, limit, offset, columns, with });
await db.query.items.findFirst({ where, ... });
await db.insert(items).values(row | rows).returning?();
await db.update(items).set(patch).where(filter).returning?();
await db.delete(items).where(filter).returning?();

where is the Drizzle 1.0 object filter: { col: value }, { col: { eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, notIn, like, ilike, notLike, notIlike, isNull, isNotNull, OR, AND, NOT } }, top-level OR/AND/NOT, relation keys ({ location: { kind: "fridge" } } or { location: true }). orderBy is { col: "asc" | "desc" }. Column, relation, and operator names in literal filters are checked at build time.

List columns (select({ multiple }), media({ multiple })) take has, isNull/isNotNull and eq: []; JSON columns (json, group, repeater, blocks) take eq/ne on the whole value and isNull/isNotNull, and neither can be ordered by. On editor collections group/repeater/blocks can’t be compared at all (their WordPress meta is spread over many rows). These are build errors with the same message the runtime returns. with: { cover: true } on a media column puts the media row in place of the id.

await on these calls compiles to plain blocking PHP calls.

Known gaps

What the design specifies and this build doesn’t do yet:

  • zero sync --watch isn’t available; run zero sync again, or from a scheduler.
  • Sync skips the columns listed under Sync; edit those through the site.

The subset (enforced at build time)

Supported: const/let, functions, arrows, closures, destructuring, spread, template literals, if/for/for...of/while/switch/try, ?., ??, objects, arrays, type annotations, type aliases, interfaces, generics (erased), structuredClone.

encodeURI(value) and encodeURIComponent(value) accept exactly one string in configuration evaluation and compiled handlers. Both preserve -_.!~*'(); only encodeURI preserves URI delimiters (;,/?:@&=+$#). They percent-encode UTF-8 bytes with uppercase hex. General JS argument coercion and decoding globals are not implemented.

Use zero check --json for machine-readable blockers. The tested compatibility inventory links specific restrictions and intentional differences to executable evidence.

Indexed array/tuple reads and destructured elements include null when an entry is missing (Zero represents undefined as PHP null). Check the fetched value or supply a default with ?? or a destructuring initializer. A non-null assertion (values[0]!) is available when your code guarantees the entry exists.

Objects and arrays have reference identity: assignment, argument passing, spreads and closures share their descendants as in JavaScript. Use structuredClone(value) for an independent graph; shared descendants and cycles survive cloning. Class instances become plain own-field objects when cloned. Captured module-level objects live for the PHP process (one web request, or the worker’s lifetime), as module data does in Node.

Arrays are dense. Writing at length appends; writing past length, at a negative or fractional index, or at NaN/Infinity throws RangeError. Grow arrays with push or Array.from({ length: n }, mapper). Zero represents undefined as null: typeof undefined gives "object", JSON.stringify({ x: undefined }) gives {"x":null}, String(undefined) gives "null", and destructuring defaults also fire on explicit null. Optional parameters include null in body reads; defaults supply missing values.

Rejected with a located error and a fix: this outside class methods or their arrows, var, enum, == (except == null), in, delete, generators, for...in, labels, getters/setters, BigInt, dynamic import(), any, eval/Function, assigning to module-level state from a hook, includes/startsWith/endsWith on a string with a position (slice first), a string lastIndexOf position other than a numeric, null or undefined literal (use a literal position or omit it; PHP erases runtime undefined into null), await on anything that isn’t a Zero API call or your own async function, an async call without await.

Build-time evaluation forbids I/O, Date.now(), new Date(), Math.random(), and db, and stops runaway loops with a step budget.

Imports: type-only imports (erased), relative .ts files (compiled with the config), and "zero". npm packages are rejected unless they ship TypeScript source that fits the subset (not implemented yet: today they’re rejected).

Classes in callbacks

Declare concrete named classes at module scope, including in relative modules with named exports. Construct them inside actions, hooks and other compiled callbacks. Public instance fields, ordinary methods, this member reads and writes, new, identity comparisons, named extends, overrides, super(...), super.method(...) and instanceof are supported. Arrows inside methods keep that method’s this. typeof Counter returns "function"; instances return "object". Extracting a prototype method is refused; use () => instance.method() when passing a callback.

class Counter {
  value = 0;
  constructor(public label: string) {}
  add(n: number): number { this.value += n; return this.value; }
  reader(): () => number { return () => this.value; }
}
class DoubleCounter extends Counter {
  add(n: number): number { return super.add(n * 2); }
}
const countVisits = action({
  input: {},
  handler: () => {
    const counter = new DoubleCounter("visits");
    const read = counter.reader();
    counter.add(2);
    return { value: read(), isCounter: counter instanceof Counter }; // 4, true
  },
});

Base fields initialize in declaration order before constructor parameter defaults. Derived fields initialize immediately after super(...), before the rest of the constructor. A derived constructor must call super(...) as its first statement; an omitted constructor forwards arguments to the parent. Public/readonly typed TypeScript parameter properties create own fields, then receive their parameter values before authored constructor statements. Defaults and other field initializers cannot read those parameter values yet, matching TypeScript’s ES2022 class-field emit. Uninitialized fields read as nullable because missing/undefined is PHP null.

Field types infer from plain data initializers; annotate fields initialized from this or calls. Parameters need a type or a primitive default. Annotate recursive, forward or overridden method returns when inference cannot establish a signature. Derived instances can pass to helpers expecting their base. Mutation effects include receivers, arguments, constructors, inherited methods and captured values; numeric updates widen literal reads and writes invalidate prior narrowing.

Static fields start from pure build-time data and live for the PHP process. Static methods inherit and dispatch with the actual class receiver. A subclass write to an inherited static field creates its own value; nested objects retain their shared identity. Static initializers cannot use runtime this, construct instances or perform I/O.

Instances retain identity through assignment, arguments and closures. JSON responses and generated client types contain own fields only; they do not include methods or class metadata. Object spread copies own fields shallowly. structuredClone, stored JSON, callback inputs and persistent once results produce plain data without class identity. Use object types in json().$type<T>(); class types and assertions that would pretend to hydrate a class are refused.

These class features remain outside the supported surface, with located errors: class expressions, default-export class declarations and anonymous/local/abstract/ambient/generic classes; decorators; private/protected/# members; accessors; static blocks; computed names; generic/rest methods; dynamic or built-in inheritance; constructor return values; prototype/reflection machinery and custom coercion/serialization protocol members. Indexed class members and recursive class field types are also refused. Uninitialized optional fields follow the same missing-to-null boundary. Class values are limited to construction, instanceof, typeof and static access. Method calls and escaping instances during construction/initialization are refused to avoid partially initialized virtual receivers. Construction and method calls inside access rules are refused; return filters from plain functions instead.

See class compilation and library reuse for the runtime representation, validation owners and the OXC/SWC assessment. This support does not enable arbitrary npm execution.

# Migrate a CMS config

`zero migrate config` imports declarative schemas from EmDash, Payload, Sanity
and the original `@spacefast/zero` capsule API (0.8.1). It writes a new
`zero.config.ts`; it never overwrites the source or an existing destination.

```sh
zero migrate config --from payload payload.config.ts --out migrated/zero.config.ts
zero build migrated
```

Use `--from emdash`, `payload`, `sanity` or `zero`. Input can be a JSON schema
export or a single TypeScript module with a default export. EmDash uses its
version `"1"` seed format; Payload uses its config's declarative object; Sanity
uses `schema.types`; original Zero uses `capsule({ collections: ... })`.
Runnable input examples live in `tests/fixtures/config-migrate`.

The importer parses TypeScript with Rust. It recognizes named imports of
Payload's `buildConfig`, Sanity's `defineConfig`/`defineType`/`defineField`/
`defineArrayMember`, and original Zero's `capsule` from
`@spacefast/zero/server`. Aliases, constants, literal objects/arrays and type
assertions work. CMS packages are never loaded. A JSON export must retain the
source declarations: `JSON.stringify` can erase callbacks before Zero sees them,
so a serialized executable config does not establish compatibility. Relative modules, spreads,
computed properties, executable statements and arbitrary helper calls require
a declarative export or a manual port. JSON and TypeScript duplicate keys fail.

## Supported mappings

| Source | Fields supported by this importer |
| --- | --- |
| EmDash | `string`, `text`, `number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `datetime`, `json` |
| Payload | `text`, `textarea`, `email`, `number`, `checkbox`, `date`, `json`, string-valued `select` (including `hasMany`) |
| Sanity | `string`, `text`, `number`, `boolean`, `datetime`; literal `initialValue`; `Rule => Rule.required()` |
| Original Zero | Content `text`, `number`, `boolean`, `datetime`, `enum` (including `multiple`), `media` (including `multiple`), single `reference` |

Required fields (including nonempty required Payload text/multi-selects and EmDash/Sanity strings),
scalar defaults, supported bounds, uniqueness and collection
labels are carried where declared. Payload's automatic `createdAt`/`updatedAt`
are generated unless `timestamps: false`. Field editor labels/descriptions are
reported for manual admin mapping. Payload's plural collection label is carried;
the loss of a distinct singular label is reported. Sanity's project/dataset
metadata and EmDash's seed metadata are identified in the report, not deployed.

EmDash integers keep Zod's safe-integer range (±9007199254740991) on top of any
declared bounds. EmDash booleans become `boolean()`, which accepts only
`true`/`false`; EmDash also accepted its stored `0`/`1`, so each boolean field is
reported for client review.

Required Payload checkboxes without an explicit default receive `false`, matching
Payload's sanitizer. Optional checkboxes keep their declared default or absence.
Required Payload JSON values must be JavaScript-truthy: `false`, `0`, `""` and
null are rejected; empty arrays and objects are allowed. Required EmDash JSON
values reject only `""`, as EmDash does for every required field. Payload text bounds use
generated validators that count UTF-16 code units, so a supplementary Unicode
character counts as two. A Payload `text` or `textarea` without `maxLength`
receives Payload's default `defaultMaxTextLength` of 40000. These validators preserve the source constraint rather
than using Zero's Unicode-character count for text `.max()`.

Field labels are preserved with `.ui({ label })` for the supported scalar and
original Zero reference mappings. Sanity field `title`/`description` map to
`label`/`help`. Payload `admin.description`, `admin.placeholder` and integer
percentage `admin.width` (for example `"50%"`) map to the same presentation
metadata. Each mapped property appears in the report. Other admin options,
including read-only behavior, are refused rather than discarded. This does not
add support for nested fields or executable admin components.

A required text field named `title` enables a WordPress custom post type with
the target's draft/revision behavior. Otherwise the imported collection uses a
SQL table (`table()` in `tables`). The report calls out this storage choice and the
need to review publishing behavior. Import does not adopt existing WordPress
post types. Original Zero's native `posts`, `pages` and `media` declarations are
refused because creating new stores would change their ownership.

An original Zero `reference` field `project` becomes an integer column
`projectId` that references the target's `id`, plus a `project` relation for
`with`. Original Zero kept a deleted target's id in place; Zero does not keep
dangling references. An optional reference is cleared when its target is
deleted (`set null`), and a required reference prevents the delete
(`restrict`). A `reference` with `multiple: true` is refused: Zero has no
multi-reference column, so model it as a join collection and move the data
yourself. Media fields keep their cardinality, and a required multiple media
field still needs at least one item.

EmDash URL fields are refused because their relative, `mailto:` and `tel:` URL
policy differs from Zero's absolute HTTP(S) URL field. Sanity URI fields are also
refused: Zero's URL validator cannot preserve Sanity's scheme/credential and
empty-value policy. Payload email fields keep Payload's own address pattern on
top of Zero's `email()` check, so quoted local parts and `[127.0.0.1]` address
literals stay rejected. Zero's `email()` also applies PHP's address check, which
rejects a local part over 64 characters or a label over 63 that Payload accepted;
each Payload email field is reported for that review. Optional Payload email fields also carry a specific
review entry because Zero rejects empty strings that Payload accepts;
null/absence remain nullable. Port or normalize that behavior before deployment.

Payload `date` fields become `timestamp()`, which accepts ISO 8601 text and
epoch milliseconds. Payload's `Date.parse` check also accepted free-form dates
such as `Jan 1 2026`; the report flags each date field so clients can send ISO.

EmDash and Sanity `datetime` fields become `timestamp()`, which accepts exactly
`YYYY-MM-DD`, or `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM[:SS[.fraction]]` with `Z` or `±HH:MM`, with
real calendar and clock values (no February 30, no `24:00`) and UTC years
0000-9999, or epoch milliseconds. It stores UTC, so values sort and filter as
times; Zero keeps milliseconds (finer fractions are truncated) and WordPress
post-backed collections keep whole seconds. Both sources stored the text as
given. Each field's report states the grammar and what changed: EmDash refused
a date alone and epoch milliseconds; Sanity accepted many other ISO 8601
spellings (week, ordinal, reduced and compact forms, expanded years, impossible
dates, no timezone, and more), which are all refused now.

JSON defaults preserve objects and arrays as distinct shapes, including empty
objects, empty arrays, and nested objects keyed `"0"`, `"1"`, ... in order.
The importer, compiled handlers and storage round trip retain those objects;
numeric property names alone do not cause a default to be refused.

Unspecified REST permissions are emitted as `false` for read/create/update/
delete, rather than inheriting Zero's public-read default. Literal Payload
boolean access rules and original Zero's `publicRead` override the corresponding
denials. Configure access before deployment. This is a reported change, not a
claim that the source CMS's authentication model has been migrated.

## Reports and refusal

The command prints JSON to stdout with `version: 1`, `source`, `status`,
`entries` and `errors`. Each entry contains an RFC 6901 `pointer`, an `outcome`
(`mapped`, `metadata` or `review`) and a `reason`. `written` means the config
compiled; review entries still require source and target behavior to be
compared. It does not mean a complete app was migrated.
Pointers address the expanded default-export object, including references to
constants. File-level errors and invalid unused declarations use the root pointer
`""`; their reason names the affected binding when applicable.

An unsupported construct exits 1 with `status: "refused"`, a pointer and reason.
No config is published. The report may contain mappings completed before the
first refusal. Invalid CLI arguments exit 2. Destination collisions also refuse;
there is no overwrite flag. The compiler validates the generated configuration
in a temporary directory before publication. Migration does not acquire plugins,
write SQL migrations to the destination or execute PHP.

The supported subset rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them. In
particular, these require a separate port:

- Access/validation/hook callbacks, except the explicit Sanity required rule.
- Rich text (Portable Text, Lexical and original Zero block bindings), CMS
  assets and references other than original Zero's single references and media
  fields, nested/custom schemas, globals, localization and custom plugins.
- EmDash documents, menus, taxonomies, settings, routes and other seed features.
- Original Zero `schema` tables, queries, mutations, actions, endpoints, pages,
  auth, connectors, sync bindings and favicon declarations.

For example, an old capsule with `queries` fails instead of producing a config
with those handlers removed. Keep the original application intact until its
behavior is implemented and validated in the new runtime.

## Config import versus application migration

For a WordPress site built with the original Zero, `zero migrate site` moves
the content after this import; see [migrating from Zero 0.8](migrating-from-zero.md).
This command does not move documents, uploads, string IDs, user identities,
sessions, secrets, URLs or browser clients. It does not convert existing PHP or
JavaScript plugins into Rust declarations. A complete old Zero migration also
needs the runtime and data work listed in the
[compatibility inventory](zero-compatibility.md).

Tests are owned by `tests/config_migrate.rs`. They run the actual command for
all four formats, build its output and load the emitted PHP schema. The
imported apps also boot on a WordPress-on-SQLite site to verify defaults,
validation and REST access. Refusal tests cover
callbacks, unknown features, dynamic code, duplicate names, invalid generated
defaults and unchanged destinations.

Reports and refusal

The command prints JSON to stdout with version: 1, source, status, entries and errors. Each entry contains an RFC 6901 pointer, an outcome (mapped, metadata or review) and a reason. written means the config compiled; review entries still require source and target behavior to be compared. It does not mean a complete app was migrated. Pointers address the expanded default-export object, including references to constants. File-level errors and invalid unused declarations use the root pointer ""; their reason names the affected binding when applicable.

An unsupported construct exits 1 with status: "refused", a pointer and reason. No config is published. The report may contain mappings completed before the first refusal. Invalid CLI arguments exit 2. Destination collisions also refuse; there is no overwrite flag. The compiler validates the generated configuration in a temporary directory before publication. Migration does not acquire plugins, write SQL migrations to the destination or execute PHP.

The supported subset rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them. In particular, these require a separate port:

  • Access/validation/hook callbacks, except the explicit Sanity required rule.
  • Rich text (Portable Text, Lexical and original Zero block bindings), CMS assets and references other than original Zero’s single references and media fields, nested/custom schemas, globals, localization and custom plugins.
  • EmDash documents, menus, taxonomies, settings, routes and other seed features.
  • Original Zero schema tables, queries, mutations, actions, endpoints, pages, auth, connectors, sync bindings and favicon declarations.

For example, an old capsule with queries fails instead of producing a config with those handlers removed. Keep the original application intact until its behavior is implemented and validated in the new runtime.

Config import versus application migration

For a WordPress site built with the original Zero, zero migrate site moves the content after this import; see migrating from Zero 0.8. This command does not move documents, uploads, string IDs, user identities, sessions, secrets, URLs or browser clients. It does not convert existing PHP or JavaScript plugins into Rust declarations. A complete old Zero migration also needs the runtime and data work listed in the compatibility inventory.

Tests are owned by tests/config_migrate.rs. They run the actual command for all four formats, build its output and load the emitted PHP schema. The imported apps also boot on a WordPress-on-SQLite site to verify defaults, validation and REST access. Refusal tests cover callbacks, unknown features, dynamic code, duplicate names, invalid generated defaults and unchanged destinations.

# Zero Identity API

The REST base is `https://site.example/wp-json/zero-identity/v1/`. Success responses are `{ "data": ... }`; failures are `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }` with an appropriate HTTP status. Responses are not cacheable. Codes, IDs and passwords are strings in JSON; timestamps are Unix seconds.

The hosted screens at `/identity` are this API's own client. A frontend app doesn't call it
directly: it signs users in through the OpenID Connect issuer below (Zero's typed client does
that for you). Registered application origins (`applications.origins`) may call this API and
the token endpoints cross-origin; every other origin is refused.

## Sign-in

| Method and path                | Body                         | Result                         |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| GET `config`                   | —                            | Providers and issuer           |
| POST `sign-in/email`           | `email`                      | `challenge_id`                 |
| POST `sign-in/verify`          | `challenge_id`, `code`       | Login result                   |
| POST `sign-in/password`        | `login`, `password`          | Login result                   |
| POST `sign-in/mfa`             | `challenge_id`, `code`       | Signed in                      |
| POST `sign-in/passkey/options` | `{}`                         | Challenge and WebAuthn options |
| POST `sign-in/passkey/verify`  | `challenge_id`, `credential` | Login result                   |

A login result is `{kind:"signed_in"}` or `{kind:"mfa_required",challenge_id}`. A primary factor never creates a session when MFA is required. The MFA challenge also requires the browser binding cookie. External providers start through `/identity/provider/start?provider=google` and return through their registered callbacks. Google is built in (`ZERO_IDENTITY_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`/`_SECRET`); add others with the `zero_identity_providers` filter (`issuer`, `client_id`, `secret`, optional `discovery`).

**Guests.** When the browser holds a session for a `zero_guest` user, `sign-in/verify` attaches the verified address to *that* user and makes it a `subscriber`: same user id, `zero_identity_guest_upgraded` fires. If the address already belongs to someone, the browser signs into that account and the guest stays as is (no merge). `GET account` reports `account.guest`.

## Organizations

GET `organizations` lists the caller's memberships. POST `organizations` accepts `name` and `idempotency_key`. Reusing the same key/name returns the same organization; changing the payload under that key fails. POST `organizations/invite` accepts `organization_id` and `email`; the inviter must be an owner/admin. POST `organizations/accept` takes the emailed `invitation` token and requires ownership of its verified address. GET `organizations/members?organization_id=...` lists members. POST `organizations/role` takes `organization_id`, `user_id`, and `role` (`owner`, `admin`, `member`); only an owner may change roles, and the last owner is protected.

## Administration

Routes below `admin/` require a native WordPress administrator, `manage_options`, a REST nonce in `X-WP-Nonce`, and the site's exact Origin on writes (registered application origins are refused here). Identity sessions do not grant WordPress administration.

Read routes: `people`, `organizations`, `applications`, `sessions`, `authentication`, `security-events`, `webhooks`. Account/session/event listings currently return up to 200 records; this is an initial administration limit, not unbounded paging.

Mutation routes: `people/suspend`, `people/erase`, `sessions/revoke`, `keys/rotate`, `webhooks`, `webhooks/remove`, and `applications`. Application registration takes `name`, `redirect_uri`, `origin` and `idempotency_key`. It permits no wildcards, fragments or callback-origin mismatches. Webhook registration returns its signing secret once.

CLI: `wp zero-identity account <id>`, `suspend`, `restore`, `revoke`, `erase`, `rotate-keys`, `webhook-add`, `webhook-remove`, `webhooks`, `maintenance`, and `wp zero-identity app add --name=<n> --redirect=<uri> --origin=<origin> [--id=<app_id>]` (an `--id` rerun with the same values returns the same app). The Abilities API gets `zero-identity/account`, a capability-checked account read.

Webhook deliveries carry `Zero-Event-Id` and `Zero-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex hmac_sha256(secret, t + "." + body)>`.

## OpenID Connect issuer

Discovery is `/identity/.well-known/openid-configuration` (also at the root `/.well-known/openid-configuration`). Applications are public clients: PKCE S256 is required, `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` is `["none"]`, and the `openid` scope, `state` and `nonce` are required.

| Endpoint | Method | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/identity/authorize` | GET, POST | Consent for a live identity session; redirects to the exact registered callback with `code` + `state` |
| `/identity/token` | POST (form) | `grant_type=authorization_code` (`code`, `redirect_uri`, `client_id`, `code_verifier`) or `grant_type=refresh_token` (`refresh_token`, `client_id`) |
| `/identity/revoke` | POST (form) | RFC 7009: `token`, `client_id`. A refresh token revokes its family, an access token its `jti`; unknown tokens succeed |
| `/identity/logout` | GET, POST | RP-initiated: `id_token_hint`, `post_logout_redirect_uri` (must share an origin with a registered callback), `state` |
| `/identity/userinfo` | GET | `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` |
| `/identity/jwks` | GET | RS256 public keys; rotated keys stay valid ten minutes |

A token response is `{ access_token, token_type: "Bearer", expires_in: 300, refresh_token, scope, id_token? }`. The access token is an RS256 JWT (`iss`, `aud` = client id, `sub` = WordPress user id, `jti`, `sid`, `exp`). The refresh token is `zr_` + 43 base64url characters, valid 30 days and **rotated on every use**: presenting one that was already used revokes its whole family and answers `400 invalid_grant`. Authorization codes are single use and live 60 seconds; a replayed code also revokes the tokens it minted. Token errors are RFC 6749 bodies `{ error, error_description }`.

**Bearer on the REST API.** `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` authenticates any WordPress REST request (a `determine_current_user` filter after core's cookie and application-password resolvers). It applies the UserInfo checks: signature, issuer, expiry, unrevoked `jti` and session, active account, enabled application. A token that fails answers `401 invalid_token`; a suspended or deleted account answers `403 suspended`.

**Guest handoff.** A guest's app holds Bearer tokens but no identity cookie. `POST /identity/handoff` with the guest's Bearer token returns `{ handoff }` (single use, 60 s). Sending the browser to `/identity/authorize?…&handoff=<handoff>` signs it in as that guest and opens the hosted screen to add an email; consent then returns to the app as usual. A handoff is bound to the guest's session and token family: revoking either first voids it. Upgrading a guest revokes all of its earlier sessions and token families, so nobody who held the guest's credentials keeps the verified account; the browser that verified gets fresh ones through consent.

**Shared connection.** Identity runs on WordPress's `$wpdb` connection. When a transaction is already open on it (the Zero runtime's, another plugin's), identity detects it and joins with savepoints instead of committing the host's work. Users whose WordPress rows identity changes are announced through `zero_identity_touched_user` so the host's rollback can clear their caches; identity clears them itself when its own savepoint or transaction rolls back.

# Zero Identity: security and operations

## Account model

The durable account identifier is `wp_users.ID`. The plugin stores normalized verified emails, provider identities, sessions, challenges and protocol records in indexed InnoDB tables. Emails use a binary unique index after ASCII lowercase/trim normalization. Internationalized email addresses are currently rejected; dots and plus tags are not rewritten. An account has one primary-email pointer. The primary address cannot be removed until another verified address becomes primary.

Existing WordPress `user_email` is a legacy recovery route. Successful email-code recovery of that address attaches it to its existing WordPress user, and duplicate legacy addresses require administrator resolution. Password checks use WordPress's password verifier. Existing WordPress roles and authored content remain attached to the same ID when the primary email changes.

Sensitive credential mutations lock account then initiating session and recheck account state, session ownership, expiry, revocation and five-minute reverification. Revocation uses the same lock order. Nested operations use savepoints. One-use challenges expire in five minutes and permit at most five attempts; invitation secrets expire in seven days. Challenge failures are committed independently before credential transactions so failed-attempt counts are not rolled back.

Guests (`zero_guest`, created by the Zero runtime) are ordinary WordPress users without an email. Verifying an email while signed in as a guest attaches it to that user; an address owned by another account never merges into a guest. Passwords, email codes, provider sign-in and passkeys all enter the same MFA gate before creating an identity session. Native WordPress password sign-in is denied for MFA-enabled accounts, directing them to Identity. Authenticator TOTP accepts only the current timestep; reuse is rejected. Recovery codes are high-entropy, hashed and single-use. A primary verified recovery address is required before removing provider/passkey credentials.

## Sessions, permissions and logout

| Credential/check                | Bound                                                   |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Identity browser session        | 24 hours, live database check on each request           |
| Sensitive-action verification   | 5 minutes                                               |
| App authorization code          | 60 seconds, single use, exact callback/client + S256    |
| App access/ID tokens            | 5 minutes                                               |
| App refresh tokens              | 30 days, rotated on every use, reuse revokes the family |

WordPress REST requests with `Authorization: Bearer` run the same live checks as UserInfo on every request, so revocation and suspension apply at once. An access token carries no WordPress capabilities of its own: the request runs as the WordPress user, with that user's role. Offline JWT validation elsewhere is not suitable for privileged operations requiring immediate revocation.

An application sign-in is one refresh family. It lives until it is revoked (`/identity/revoke`, RP logout, global revocation, password change, suspension) or its refresh token goes unused for 30 days. The identity session's 24-hour expiry bounds the hosted screens, not the families it started. Refresh tokens and authorization codes are stored as SHA-256 digests. A rotated refresh token is kept with `used_at`/`replaced_by`, so presenting it again is detected as theft and ends the family.

Identity session secrets contain 256 random bits and are stored as domain-separated SHA-256 digests. They do not depend on WordPress salts. WordPress salts protect challenges and encrypted secrets (signing keys, MFA secrets, webhook secrets): **rotating the `SECURE_AUTH` salt makes them unreadable**. Back up salts with the database; fixing this with a sealed root key of the plugin's own is a follow-up.

## Browser and protocol boundaries

Cookie-authenticated writes require the canonical identity Origin or a registered application origin (`applications.origins`, an exact `scheme://host[:port]`). Other origins fail; WordPress's reflected credentialed CORS headers are replaced in this REST namespace by headers for registered origins only. The token and revoke endpoints answer CORS for registered origins without credentials. Sensitive writes use session CSRF tokens. Consent checks Origin and CSRF. `prompt=login`/`max_age` require a new browser sign-in before consent; silent `prompt=none` is not supported.

Incoming OIDC requires provider-pinned algorithms, validated JWKS keys, exact issuer/audience, nonce and time checks. Provider identities use immutable issuer + subject. UserInfo and ID-token subjects must agree. Code, PKCE, state, browser-bound challenge and replay checks are independent.

Deploy behind HTTPS with the correct trusted proxy configuration. Exclude identity HTML/API from shared caches. The development HTTP override requires both `ZERO_IDENTITY_DEV_HTTP=true` and WordPress's `local` environment; do not enable it on public deployments.

## Maintenance and diagnostics

`wp zero-identity maintenance` sends at most 30 due webhook deliveries per run. A delivery gets a two-minute processing lease, up to eight attempts and exponential retry delays. Delivery is at least once: consumers deduplicate by `Zero-Event-Id`. Requests do not follow redirects and WordPress's safe HTTP client rejects private-network destinations.

The signature header is `Zero-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256>`. Verify HMAC over the exact bytes `<timestamp>.<body>`, use constant-time comparison, and reject stale timestamps such as those older than five minutes. Store the signing secret securely. **Identity → Authentication** shows recent status/attempts; it displays a new secret only once. CLI equivalents are `wp zero-identity webhook-add <https-url>`, `webhooks`, and `webhook-remove <id>`.

Use a real cron scheduler every minute for reliable retries; the fallback WordPress event is hourly and depends on traffic. Monitor `email.accepted`/`email.failed`, `provider.rejected`, account/session events and webhook HTTP statuses. Email acceptance indicates `wp_mail` transport acceptance only. SMTP delivery, bounce handling and inbox acceptance remain transport responsibilities. Authentication rate limits are stored in the database and use both network and account buckets.

Rotate signing keys with `wp zero-identity rotate-keys`. Back up the database and WordPress salts together. Changing secure-auth salts makes stored encrypted secrets unreadable and requires explicit operational recovery. Never log codes, cookies, tokens, private keys or client secrets.

## Privacy and lifecycle

Users export their profile, connections, session metadata, organization memberships, passkey metadata and events. Exports omit credential secrets. Deletion requests immediately suspend the local account. An administrator completes erasure from People or `wp zero-identity erase <id>`. Sole organization owners must transfer ownership, and WordPress administrators must transfer administration first. Erasure removes identity credentials and metadata, anonymizes the WordPress account, removes roles and preserves authored content under the retained numeric author ID. It is idempotent. WordPress privacy exporter/eraser callbacks are registered.

Uninstall preserves all data. Backups, external webhook recipients and other plugins' metadata have separate retention policies. V1 uses English UI copy; full localization and enterprise federation/provisioning are not claimed.

The deletion request checks sole-owner status before suspension, so an owner can still sign in and transfer ownership. The erasure transaction repeats the ownership check to handle changes after the request.
