# Migrating from Zero 0.8

This guide moves a WordPress site built with the original `@spacefast/zero`
0.8 (`capsule()` collections) onto the new Zero: the same posts, ids, fields,
media, revisions and authors, now served by the `zero-app-<name>` plugin at
`/wp-json/zero/v1`.

It takes two commands. `zero migrate config` turns the capsule into a
`zero.config.ts`, and `zero migrate site` moves the content in place. Both
refuse anything they can't carry and name the exact spot, so nothing is
silently dropped.

## Before you start

- Back up the database. The site migration runs in one transaction and rolls
  back on any refusal, but a backup is still the undo button.
- Find the original release: the `content-model.php` the original runtime
  activated for your Space, under
  `<private root>/spaces/<space>/content-model/releases/<revision>/`.
  It names every collection and field the site stored. It is PHP the original
  compiler generated, and the command runs it on the site as `wp eval-file`
  would, dry run included. Use only that file, never one from somewhere else.
- Keep the original app's code. Queries, mutations, actions, endpoints, pages
  and sign-in are not migrated here; see [what stays manual](#what-stays-manual).

## 1. Convert the config

```sh
zero migrate config --from zero capsule.ts --out app/zero.config.ts
```

The report (JSON on stdout) lists every mapping and every review item. Each
collection becomes a WordPress post type `zero_<name>`, and each field a
column:

| Original field | New column |
| --- | --- |
| `text` (`multiline`, `maxLength`) | `text()` with the same bound |
| `number` | `real()` |
| `boolean` | `boolean()` |
| `datetime` | `timestamp()` |
| `enum` / `enum` + `multiple` | `select()` |
| `media` / `media` + `multiple` | `media()` / `media({ multiple: true })` |
| `reference` to `projects` | `projectId: integer().references(...)` plus a `project` relation |

Original Zero kept a deleted target's id in a reference. The new Zero doesn't
keep dangling ids: an optional reference is cleared when its target goes
(`set null`), and a required one blocks the delete (`restrict`).

See [config migration](config-migration.md) for the full rules.

## 2. Review access

The importer denies every write until you say otherwise, and only carries
`publicRead` over to reads. Open the new config and set `access` on each
collection, for example:

```ts
{ access: { read: true, create: "editor", update: "editor", delete: "editor" } }
```

## 3. Build and activate

```sh
zero build app
```

Deactivate the original runtime, upload `app/.zero/wp-content/plugins/`, and
activate the dependencies, then `zero-runtime`, then `zero-app-<name>`. The new
post types exist now, but your content is still tagged with the original
`zero_collection` taxonomy, so they're empty.

## 3½. Copy the uploads

The original platform kept a Space's uploads in its private storage root
(`<private root>/spaces/<space>/content-media/`), not in `wp-content/uploads`,
and served them itself. Copy that folder's contents into `wp-content/uploads`,
keeping the `YYYY/MM/` paths, so WordPress can serve the same attachments.
The migration checks every media file it carries over and refuses with the
record and field if one is missing.

## 4. Dry run

```sh
zero migrate site content-model.php --dry-run --wp "wp --path=/srv/site"
```

`--wp` is any WP-CLI command that reaches the site: `wp --ssh=host:/path`,
`docker compose exec -T cli wp`, and so on. The release is sent on stdin, so the
file stays on your machine. Without `--wp`, the command targets the local test
harness.

The report lists each collection's record ids, how many revisions come along,
what's skipped (trashed posts stay in the trash, untouched), and review notes
(a `pending` or `private` post keeps its WordPress status, and reads as a draft).
No content is written: the dry run plans inside a transaction and rolls it back.

## 5. Migrate

```sh
zero migrate site content-model.php --wp "wp --path=/srv/site"
```

Each record keeps its post id, so references, media ids, comments and links
stay valid. Its post type becomes `zero_<name>`, and every
`_zero_<collection>_<field>` value is rewritten as the new `zero_<column>`
field. Status, publish dates, scheduled times and authors are the post row's
own and don't change. A column you added in step 2 starts at its default. Revisions keep their author and date, and gain the
record's field values, so restoring one changes the title the way it did before.

Run it again any time: migrated posts no longer carry the original tag, so a
second run finds nothing to do. The run is one database transaction, so a
failure partway leaves the site exactly as it was. It needs InnoDB tables for
posts, post meta and terms, and refuses to start otherwise.

Only the original collection tag is removed. Categories and tags a post
carried stay attached, and the original collection terms stay too (counted
again), so the original app's data model is still there to roll back to.

If the site hosted more than one original Space, pass `--space=<id>`. The
command refuses to guess.

## 6. App users (optional)

If the original Space had sign-in, its app users are already WordPress users:
the identity plugin's accounts, marked as members of the Space. To make them
members of the new app, register a `userProjection()` in `users` (see
`docs/config-api.md`), build and activate it, then run:

```sh
wp zero migrate-legacy-users --space=<id> --dry-run
wp zero migrate-legacy-users --space=<id>
```

Activate zero-identity first: the command carries each account's state into
it. Each app user keeps their WordPress id, password and role. Their verified
primary email becomes the member's email and their zero-identity email, and
their account status carries over, so a user suspended on the original platform
stays suspended (and one already suspended or erased in the new app stays so).
The member collection's own columns start at their defaults (a column without
one starts empty), validated like any write with the user's role in view. A
reference, media or file column can't take a default here, so set those after
the move. An app user without a verified email refuses the run with
`/users/<id>/email`. So does a unique value (`/users/<id>/<column>`, the email
included) that another user holds, or that an earlier user in the same run just
took, compared the way the database compares (`Invite` and `invite` are one
value). Nothing
changes on a refusal, and the dry run catches all of these. A second run skips
users already moved. Original Zero guests lived only in the browser, so there
are none to move.

## Refusals

A refusal is a JSON problem with an RFC 6901 pointer, and the whole run rolls
back:

| Pointer | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `""` | the site holds several original Spaces (pass `--space`), or a table isn't InnoDB |
| `/postTypes/3/id` | that collection has no counterpart in the new config, is a `table()`, localized, `uid`/`sync` or has a `slug()` column, or has a new column whose default the migration can't write (post content, references, media, files, structured fields) |
| `/postTypes/3/fields/2/name` | the field's column is missing, or is the new app's `content` or `slug` column |
| `/postTypes/3/fields/2/definition` | the field's type or options don't match the new column |
| `/postTypes/3/fields/2/definition/type` | rich text and blocks fields need a content port |
| `/records/42/project` | record 42's reference points at a post that isn't a live project |
| `/records/42/gallery/1` | the second media id isn't an attachment, isn't an image (for an image-only column), or its file isn't in `wp-content/uploads` yet |
| `/records/42/title` | a value breaks a rule of the new column (required, bound), or repeats a unique value among the records or the collection's live rows |

Fix the data in WordPress (or the new config), then run again.

## What stays manual

The config and content migration don't move:

- `blocks` (rich text) fields and multiple references. The importer refuses them.
- Native `posts`, `pages` and `media` collections.
- `schema` tables, queries, mutations, actions, endpoints, pages, islands,
  connectors and sync bindings: port them to `zero.config.ts` actions and hooks.
- Sign-in providers and sessions of the original platform (app users themselves move with step 6).
- The original Space's routes, redirects and private file storage.

The [compatibility inventory](zero-compatibility.md) tracks each of these.

# Zero PHP runtime contract

The Rust compiler (`zero build`) emits WordPress plugins. Everything that runs
at request time is PHP: a hand-written runtime library (`runtime/Zero/*.php`,
copied verbatim into every build) plus generated files. This document is the
seam between them. The compiler only emits calls listed here.

Requirements (`Platform::problems()` is the one statement of them; activation
and `zero doctor` both apply it): WordPress 7.1+ on PHP 8.2+ with the
`mbstring`, `json` and `gd` extensions (`sodium` for the identity bundle);
MySQL 8.0+ or MariaDB 10.11+ with every Zero table InnoDB, or SQLite through
SQLite Database Integration 3.1.2+; the pinned platform plugins Secure Custom
Fields, Action Scheduler and MCP Adapter at the versions in
`Platform::PLUGINS`, plus Polylang when the app is localized. Composer runs
only at maintainer time; prefixed third-party libraries ship under
`vendor-prefixed/`. See `dependencies.md` for their locks and regeneration.
Every Zero file starts with `declare(strict_types=1);`. Namespace `Zero`.

## Build output layout

```
<out>/                                 (default: <project>/.zero/wp-content)
  zero-manifest.json                   versions, runtime series, platform requirements, dependency checksums
  plugins/zero-runtime/
    zero-runtime.php                   plugin header; boots Wp\Plugin
    zero/*.php                         this library, copied verbatim
    zero/vendor-prefixed/**            bundled, isolated PHP dependencies
  plugins/zero-identity/               optional identity bundle (passkeys, sessions, tokens)
  plugins/zero-app-<name>/
    zero-app-<name>.php                plugin header
    zero/app/schema.php                generated: `return [...]` schema metadata
    zero/app/functions.php             generated: compiled hooks, actions, helpers (namespace ZeroApp)
    zero/app/migrations/NNNN_<name>.sql  MySQL DDL, `{prefix}` for the table prefix
    public/...                         copied from <project>/public if present
  *.zip                                the same plugins, packaged
```

`zero/bootstrap.php` eagerly loads `Db.php` (for the `Zero\db()` function),
sets `ini_set('precision', '-1')`, `ini_set('serialize_precision', '-1')`,
registers an autoloader for `Zero\*` from its own directory, and registers the
ordered feature modules through `Features::register()` (once per process).

The signing key for private-file URLs is the `zero_runtime_secret` option,
minted on activation.

The app's schema is the authoritative runtime series check; the runtime
refuses a mismatched series or a second app plugin.

`GET /_schema` on WordPress includes `runtime.wp` with WordPress/PHP/database
versions, `scf`, `actionScheduler`, `mcpAdapter`, `polylang`, `identity`,
`imageCdn`, and `incompatibleTables`. `runtime.pendingMigrations` and
`runtime.languages` report app migration and localization state. Identity is
true only for a compatible implementation; the A3 placeholder does not enable it.
`zero doctor [--site URL --token T]` checks this data against the same
platform policy used by runtime activation.

## schema.php

```php
return [
  'collections' => [
    'items' => [
      'primaryKey' => 'id',
      'columns' => [
        // type: 'integer' | 'real' | 'text' | 'boolean' | 'timestamp' | 'date' | 'json'
        'id'        => ['type' => 'integer', 'primaryKey' => true, 'autoIncrement' => true, 'notNull' => true],
        'name'      => ['type' => 'text', 'notNull' => true],
        'unit'      => ['type' => 'text', 'notNull' => true, 'enum' => ['pcs', 'g'], 'default' => ['value' => 'pcs']],
        'quantity'  => ['type' => 'integer', 'notNull' => true, 'default' => ['value' => 1]],

## functions.php

Generated. `namespace ZeroApp;`. Contains plain PHP functions. The runtime
calls them by the names in schema.php (prefix `\ZeroApp\`):

| Compiled callback | Call | Return handling |
|---|---|---|
| beforeCreate | `$r = $fn($data, $ctx)` | a `JsObject` replaces data; otherwise retain mutations to `$data` |
| afterCreate | `$fn($row, $ctx)` | ignored |
| beforeUpdate | `$r = $fn($patch, $existing, $ctx)` | a `JsObject` replaces the patch; otherwise retain mutations to `$patch` |
| afterUpdate | `$fn($row, $previous, $ctx)` | ignored |
| beforeDelete / afterDelete | `$fn($row, $ctx)` | ignored |
| default fn / onUpdate fn | `$v = $fn()` | converted through `Seam::generated` for the column |
| action handler | `$out = $fn($input)` | converted to wire values and returned as `data` |

A string in a schema callback slot names compiled code. `Seam` converts its
schema-shaped input and context to `JsObject` / `JsArray` handles. Each callback
receives a fresh graph; before-hooks' `$data` / `$patch` shares identity with
`$ctx->p['data']`, so in-place mutations are retained without a replacement
return. After-hook and delete-hook return values are ignored. Native non-string
callables retain PHP array inputs and contexts; before-hooks replace data or
patches only when their return is a native array.

Compiled object and array parameters pass handles by value: member mutations
are shared, but rebinding a parameter does not replace the caller's binding.
Captured bindings retain that JavaScript behavior, including arrays, open
records and optional fields. Object spread/rest copies field values shallowly.
Loop-local declarations receive a fresh binding on each execution, and a
captured `for (let …)` header variable receives a fresh `Js::cell` per iteration.
The cell copies its value; copying a handle preserves the referenced container.

Arrays remain dense. Indexed writes may replace an existing element or append
at the current length; writes past the end throw a catchable `RangeError`.
Writing through a missing receiver throws `TypeError`. Assignments evaluate
the receiver and key before the value; read-modify-write operations read the
old value before evaluating the right-hand side. These are runtime semantics,
not a blanket refusal of writes into array elements.

## Compiled classes

Generated class methods are plain `ZeroApp` functions with an explicit first
receiver argument. They use `JsObject` handles for instances, so aliases,
closures, member mutations and strict identity use the existing object model.
`JsObject::$class` is readonly descriptor metadata; only `JsObject::$p` contains
enumerable own fields. PHP inheritance and PHP method binding are not used.

`JsClass` descriptors contain the parent, constructor and ordered field
initializer closures, instance/static method tables, and a static `JsObject`.
Generated descriptor factory functions cache one descriptor per class per process.
The compiler emits these runtime operations:

- `construct(...$args): JsObject` allocates a fresh handle and initializes it.
- `initialize(JsObject $instance, array $args): void` runs a constructor on the
  existing receiver. Base fields precede constructor defaults; generated derived
  constructors call the parent's initializer, then their own field initializer.
- `invoke($receiver, $name, $args, $static): mixed` selects the actual receiver's
  descriptor. `invokeOn(...)` starts at the lexical parent for `super` calls while
  retaining that receiver. Methods receive the hidden receiver explicitly.
- `get`, `has` and `set` implement static field inheritance. Reads search parents;
  writes create an own field on the actual class descriptor.
- `isInstance($value, $expected): bool` walks descriptor ancestry, never field
  shapes. Plain/cloned/deserialized objects do not acquire class identity.

`Js::prop`, `has` and `set` also accept descriptors for compiled static field
updates. Spread, object keys and JSON visit own properties only. `Js::clone`
and `Seam` detachment copy the own-field graph into plain handles; descriptors
and method tables are not traversed or serialized. Generated client types erase
instance identity recursively at the wire boundary.

## Write pipeline (`Db::insert/update/delete`, REST and CLI all go through it)

Viewer-bound writes must not answer existence questions about unreadable data.
Setting a non-null unique value (including an explicit primary key or a generated
slug) requires an unfiltered collection read rule and visibility of that field
across rows. Otherwise both taken and free values return 401/403 before any
uniqueness lookup. A filtered read, including `self` or automatic draft filtering,
does not authorize new or changed unique values. An unchanged value is accepted
only when the viewer can read the current row and the column cannot hide values.
That value is omitted from persistence, and native slug repair preserves it without
querying competitors. Publishing a WordPress draft is a new uniqueness operation;
echoing or omitting its slug cannot bypass the full visibility preflight.
Hidden columns and unreadable rows receive the same refusal
before equality can affect the response. Trusted CLI/hook writes retain normal
uniqueness checks; successful public creates retain their ordinary row response.
System uids remain unguessable sync identities.

Blind intake belongs in a narrow application action, not a public unique-create
endpoint. The site example acknowledges newsletter requests with a constant
response and queues private, deduplicated processing; it returns neither a
subscriber row nor a job identifier. Existing and new subscriptions have the
same acknowledgement. Exact announcement recipient counts are admin-only,
including filtering: comparing counts around a signup would otherwise disclose
membership. Member administrators explicitly have collection read
access before managing unique identities. Its editor-only removal action
authorizes detaching private subscription links and returns only the post id;
private subscriber data never leaves that action. These application policies
do not exempt viewer-bound CRUD from the checks above.

Every reference in a viewer-bound write, including generated values, must resolve within the target's read filters and use
a readable target column; an unreadable target and a missing target return the
same `reference_violation`, without the resolved value in its detail. Knowing a
sync UID grants no target visibility: primary and non-primary references both
require a viewer-scoped lookup, and the write pipeline checks visibility again
after hooks. Hidden and absent translation peers both remain unlinked until a
visible peer is available. This applies to core WordPress saves too.
Sync checks target visibility before resolved values reach input rules or validators.
Potential generated constraints are preflighted before defaults and on-update
generators run; hook-written references are checked before field validation.
A delete requires visibility across the referencing collection and
column before checking for children, so hidden children cannot be discovered by
trying to delete their parent. The preflight follows cascade branches and covers
generated values from referential updates even when a branch has no rows. Hidden
cascade branches are refused before traversal, so recursion limits cannot reveal
their depth.
These checks roll back the whole write on refusal.
Changing a referenced key uses the same relationship visibility preflight,
following native cascading updates before the database can expose hidden children.
Native WordPress draft publication preflights slug visibility before collision
resolution. Wrapped saves and editor forms preserve an omitted slug on an
already published, scheduled, or private row. Programmatic native writes without
known input provenance retain collision resolution and require slug visibility.

Create, per row:
1. Let registered input normalizers consume virtual inputs, then reject unknown keys
   (`invalid_input`, pointer `/<key>`). The original supplied input remains available to write hooks.
2. Apply defaults for absent keys: `value`, `now` (current UTC timestamp, or
   today's date for `date`), `fn`.
   2b. A required column (notNull, no default, not autoIncrement) that is
   absent and not listed in the collection's `beforeCreateFills` →
   `invalid_input` pointer `/<col>`. Hooks never see a missing required field.
3. `beforeCreate`.
4. Validate + coerce every column (below). Missing required (notNull, no
   default, not autoIncrement) → `invalid_input` pointer `/<col>`.
5. INSERT. UNIQUE violation → 409 `unique_violation` with pointer `/<col>`
   when the column can be determined. FK violation → 409 `reference_violation`.
6. Re-read the row by primary key → `afterCreate($row)`.

Update, per matching row (rows are selected first, then updated by PK):
1. Normalize virtual input, then reject unknown keys and changing the primary key.
2. For columns with `onUpdate` that are absent from the patch, set them.
3. `beforeUpdate($patch, $existing)`.
4. Validate + coerce patched columns.
5. UPDATE by PK; re-read → `afterUpdate($row, $previous)`.

Delete, per matching row: `beforeDelete($row)`, DELETE by PK, `afterDelete($row)`.

Writes made by hooks or actions through `Db` run the same pipeline
(including hooks). Nesting deeper than 8 levels → `HttpError(500, 'hook_recursion', ...)`.

Every HTTP request and every CLI command runs in one transaction
(`START TRANSACTION`, REPEATABLE READ). An exception before the commit rolls
back every write of the request. Two things are outside that guarantee: an
`afterCommit` callback runs after the commit, so its failure propagates without
undoing the request; and `wp zero migrate` records each DDL statement as it
succeeds (MySQL DDL commits implicitly), so a later statement's failure leaves
the earlier ones applied and recorded (see Migrations).
Transactions run concurrently, so a read whose result the transaction then
depends on takes an explicit lock (`FOR UPDATE`, `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`; see
`Sync\Lock`, `Locale\Lock`, `Jobs\Storage`).

## Validation and coercion (input → stored)

| type | accepts | stored as (custom table column) |
|---|---|---|
| integer | int, or a float with no fractional part whose magnitude is at most 9007199254740991 (JavaScript's safe-integer range) | BIGINT |
| real | int or float (not NaN/Inf) | DOUBLE |
| text | string | LONGTEXT (VARCHAR when unique or bounded) |
| boolean | bool | TINYINT(1) 0/1 |
| timestamp | int ms, or ISO 8601 `YYYY-MM-DD` (UTC midnight) / `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm[:ss[.fff]]` + `Z` or `±HH:MM`, every component a real calendar/clock value (no `now`, `10/30/2026`, zone-less date-times or `02-30`) | TEXT `Y-m-d\TH:i:s.v\Z` (UTC) |
| date | string `YYYY-MM-DD` that is a real calendar date | CHAR(10) |
| json | any JSON value | LONGTEXT (json_encode, unescaped slashes/unicode) |

`enum` → value must be one of the listed strings. `null` is accepted only
when not `notNull`. Wrong type → `invalid_input` with pointer `/<col>` and
a detail naming the expected type.

Reading rows back (decode): integer → int, real → float, boolean → bool,
json → decoded (assoc arrays), others → string, NULL → null. Every row
returned anywhere (REST, Db, hooks) has every column key present.

## class Db

```php
final class Db {
  public static function instance(): Db;            // set up by App::boot
  public function findMany(string $collection, array $opts = []): array;   // list<row>
  public function findFirst(string $collection, array $opts = []): ?array; // findMany with limit 1
  public function insert(string $collection, array $values, bool $returning = false): ?array;
  public function update(string $collection, array $set, array $where, bool $returning = false): ?array;
  public function delete(string $collection, array $where, bool $returning = false): ?array;
}
function db(): Db;   // namespace Zero, in Db.php, returns Db::instance()
```

`insert` `$values`: one row (assoc array) or a list of rows. With
`$returning`, insert/update/delete return a list of the affected rows
(post-write rows for insert/update, pre-delete rows for delete); otherwise
`null`.

`$opts` (Drizzle relational-query v1 shape):

- `where`: filter (below).
- `orderBy`: `['name' => 'asc', 'createdAt' => 'desc']`.
- `limit`, `offset`: ints.
- `columns`: `['id' => true, 'name' => true]` → only those keys.
- `with`: `['location' => true, 'items' => ['where' => ..., 'orderBy' => ..., 'limit' => ..., 'with' => ...]]`.
  `one` relations attach a row or null; `many` attach a list. Load with one
  extra query per relation per level (`WHERE fk IN (...)`), never N+1.

Filter grammar:

- `['col' => scalar]` → `col = ?`; `['col' => null]` → `col IS NULL`.
- `['col' => ['eq' => v, 'ne' => v, 'gt' => v, 'gte' => v, 'lt' => v, 'lte' => v,
  'in' => [..], 'notIn' => [..], 'like' => s, 'notLike' => s, 'ilike' => s,
  'notIlike' => s, 'isNull' => true, 'isNotNull' => true,
  'NOT' => fieldFilter, 'OR' => [fieldFilter..], 'AND' => [fieldFilter..]]]`
  (several operators in one object are ANDed).
- Top level `'OR' => [filter..]`, `'AND' => [filter..]`, `'NOT' => filter`.
- Relation key: `['location' => true]` → related row exists;
  `['location' => filter]` → EXISTS related row matching filter.
- Values are coerced with the column's encoder (booleans → 0/1, timestamps
  normalized). `like` is case-sensitive, `ilike` case-insensitive.
- Unknown column/relation/operator → `HttpError(400, 'invalid_query', ...)` with pointer
  like `/where/qty`.

All values are bound parameters. Identifiers come only from schema.php.

## Runtime extension points (schema v3)

`Features` owns the ordered module list; bootstrap registers it once. A module
registers callbacks through `Extensions`, plus idempotent dialect-specific DDL
through `SystemTables` when needed. Registration itself performs no app I/O.

- `beforeRead(collection, &opts, ?viewer, pointer)` runs before query validation
  and SQL; its normalized options also govern projection at every relation level.
  Constraint preflights treat extension narrowing as filtered visibility: unique
  namespaces, generated references, and incoming relationships must remain fully
  readable before storage can answer about competitors or children. Unchanged
  unique values must also survive a viewer-scoped read of the current row.
  Custom `beforeRead` and `onRead` callbacks conservatively disable viewer-bound
  namespace checks, since an arbitrary callback can hide values conditionally.
  A registration may set `constraintSafe: true` only when its visibility policy
  preserves row membership and constraint columns except for restrictions already
  represented by schema access rules; built-in transforms do so.
  Concrete references still require a row and matching column value in the final
  viewer-visible result, including read transforms. Trusted writes remain available.
  `onLookup(collection, pks)` runs in concrete stores before hydration
  and decode. Lookup receives nonempty collection pages, not system-media rows.
  Mutation results (including receipt replay) and revision snapshots also prime
  their page before read transforms; callbacks may run again after write hooks.
- `onRead(rows, collection, ?viewer)` transforms decoded rows before `with` and
  projection; also applies to revision reads and returning write responses.
  Revision restore authorizes first, then uses the full stored snapshot; display
  transforms never supply persistence input. Internal mutation selection keeps
  authorization filters and passes full decoded storage rows to normalization,
  validation and write hooks, including previous-row notifications.
  Keep primary keys intact. Relation attachment preserves original linkage
  privately; removing a media column prevents its population.
- `normalizeWrite(op, collection, &data, ?existing, ?viewer, provided)` consumes
  virtual inputs before column rejection on create/update. Keep it free of
  persisted effects; unconsumed unknown keys remain errors.
- `onWrite(op, collection, &data, ?existing, ?viewer, provided)` runs after
  defaults/onUpdate and before app before-hooks (create: also before required
  and access checks). `provided` is the original row/patch. Delete runs before
  `beforeDelete`. `onWritten(op, collection, row, ?previous)` runs after app
  after-hooks in the same transaction, including WP editor notifications.
  WP editor captures use `editorRow(collection, pk)` to keep full stored values
  for previous/deleted rows, even when trusted reads have display transforms.
- `afterCommit(fn)` delegates to the active Db's Store. The outermost commit
  drains its queue; rollback discards it. Outside a transaction it runs
  immediately. Nested transactions join without savepoints. A callback that
  throws propagates after commit, without rollback cleanup or callback replay.
- `route(prefix, handler)` receives `(method, fullDecodedSegments, query,
  rawBody, viewer, files, form)` and returns `[status, data]` or `Response`. One
  complete first segment is matched before built-ins and collections. Thus the
  auth feature can replace `/auth/token`; without a registered owner the phase-1
  login remains. A module that owns a prefix owns all its dispatch and method checks.
- `beforeAction(spec, name, rawBody, headers, ?viewer)` sees exact input bytes
  and lowercase header names after action authorization, before input validation.
  JSON syntax parsing retains its phase-1 precedence before action lookup.
  HTTP and CLI actions share this path; a null viewer means trusted CLI.
- `aroundOperation(scope, spec, rawBody, headers, ?viewer, next): Response` wraps
  `action:<name>` and HTTP `create:<collection>` in the current transaction.
  Action authorization, raw-body guards and input validation, or create input
  normalization/required/access checks, run before wrappers, including on replay.
  Calling `next()` executes the handler/write pipeline. A wrapper may instead
  return its stored result and add metadata with `Response::withHeaders`.
  Wrapper failures roll back both writes and receipt effects. Create wrappers
  see the full persisted row; read transforms apply after execution or replay.
  `Db::insert` exposes its optional per-row `around(callable(): array): array`
  continuation to the request adapter. Trusted nested writes do not inherit
  the request header or create another receipt.
- HTTP list and item reads forward feature query options to `beforeRead`. The
  feature consumes/normalizes its options; unknown remaining options fail normal
  query validation.
- `cli(command, handler)` receives `(argsWithoutCommand, flags)` inside the
  canonical `wp zero` transaction and receipts.
- `schemaDescribe(fn)` transforms the public schema description.

`SystemTables::register(name, statements)` assigns one owner per table. The
list contains idempotent SQL strings (`{prefix}` is the WordPress table prefix)
or guarded `callable(Store): void` upgrades (a column check against
`information_schema` before `ADD COLUMN`). `apply(Store)` rejects request
transactions before running SQL or guards; the runtime applies registrations
on activation and on the first request after an update, outside request
transactions. `Store` exposes `afterCommit(callable)` and
`applySystemStatements(list<string>)` for these seams.

`Wp\Scf::fieldFilter(fn)` transforms each fully-built field, including nested
fields, with `(field, definition, column, spec)`. Top-level `spec` is the
collection/global; nested `spec.fields` contains sibling definitions.

Schema loading requires v3 and runtime series `0.3`; v2 and missing or
incompatible series are refused with a rebuild instruction. Series `0.3`
requires handle-based compiled callbacks; schemas from the `0.2` compiler
cannot load under this runtime. `Schema::version()` and
`Schema::runtime()` report the loaded contract. New feature metadata passes
through unchanged; feature modules own its behavior. Lazy scheduled promotion
remains at the start of requests/commands, so due records are visible in that
same request.

`App::dispatch(method, path, query, rawBody, Viewer, headers = [], files = [],
form = []): Response` is the shared operation entry point for HTTP and Abilities.
It opens or joins a transaction, promotes due rows, binds the explicit viewer
as hook actor, and restores the previous actor even on failure. It does not
resolve credentials or convert exceptions to HTTP problems. `App::invoke(method,
path, query, body, Viewer)` is its data-only convenience for JSON operations;
`body` is a decoded value or exact raw JSON string. Headers and raw file responses
use `dispatch`. HTTP resolves credentials once, then uses the same dispatcher.

`Response::json(data, status = 200, headers = [])` keeps the normal `{data}`
envelope. `Response::raw(string|Closure, status = 200, headers = [])` returns
bytes or a deferred emitter for downloads. Raw handlers set their content type
and download/security/cache headers explicitly. Both HTTP transports emit only
after the operation transaction commits. `App::handle` returns a string or
closure body; the WordPress REST adapter calls `Response::emit`.
Stream emitters perform I/O only, with authorization/file readiness already
checked in the transaction. Streaming errors cannot roll back a committed
operation or replace an already-started response.

## Migrations

`Wp\Migrator` applies the app plugin's `zero/app/migrations/NNNN_<name>.sql`
files (MySQL dialect, `{prefix}` replaced by `$wpdb->prefix`) in filename
order. Statements are separated by a line `--> statement-breakpoint`. The
ledger is `{prefix}zero__migrations(app, id, applied_at)`, keyed by app so two
plugins' `0001_init` files stay apart. MySQL DDL commits implicitly, so every
statement that succeeds is recorded as `<id>:<n>` before the next one runs;
once a file completes its own id is recorded and the step rows are removed. A
file that failed half way resumes at the failing statement. A statement that
committed without its marker fails on the retry ("already exists") until the
operator records it with `wp zero migrate --mark-applied <id>:<n>`. Writers
(first request, activation, `wp zero migrate`) serialize on `Connection::locked`.

## class Js — JavaScript semantics in PHP

Static methods on `final class Js`. Value model: JS `number` = PHP
`int|float`; `string` = PHP `string` (UTF-8; indexes count UTF-16 code units; splitting a surrogate pair throws `RangeError`); `boolean` = `bool`; `null` and `undefined` are both PHP `null`;
arrays are `Zero\JsArray`, plain objects are `Zero\JsObject`, both handles
with identity; class instances are `JsObject` handles with a non-enumerable
`JsClass` descriptor; functions are `Closure`; `Date` values are numbers (epoch ms); `RegExp` is `Zero\RegExp`.
The compiler emits native PHP whenever types make it safe; these helpers
cover the cases where JS and PHP genuinely differ. Each must match the
JavaScript result exactly on the inputs its types allow.

Configuration evaluation uses the same UTF-16 units for numeric string indexes,
`slice` and `split("")`; a result containing a lone surrogate is rejected with a
located build diagnostic. `split` applies its limit before converting units.

String `lastIndexOf` accepts only literal number/null/undefined positions; a
runtime position can hide the erased null/undefined distinction behind an alias,
assertion or call. Omit the position or use a literal instead.

Conversions:
- `str(mixed $v): string` — `String(v)`. null → `"null"`, bools → `"true"/"false"`, numbers → `numStr`, list → elements `str`'d joined by `,` with null as `""`, assoc → `"[object Object]"`, `RegExp` → `/src/flags`.
- `numStr(int|float $n): string` — `Number.prototype.toString()`: `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `-0` → `"0"`, integral values below 1e21 without exponent, shortest round-trip digits, exponent form `1e+21`, `1.5e-7` exactly where JS uses it (≥ 1e21 or < 1e-6).
- `toNumber(mixed $v): int|float` — `Number(v)`: null → 0, bool → 0/1, string trimmed of JS whitespace: `""` → 0, decimal, `0x`/`0o`/`0b` prefixes, `Infinity`/`-Infinity`, otherwise NAN. Safe integers (|n| ≤ 2^53) return int, larger values float.
- `n(int|float $r): int|float` — an int as a JS number: beyond ±2^53 it becomes the nearest double. Compiled `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` and unary `-a` on numbers are `add`/`sub`/`mul`/`neg`, which take each operand through `n()` and then the result; `++`/`--` are `preStep`/`postStep(&$x, ±1)` (the place is evaluated once), and `**`/`Math.pow` are `pow(a, b)`. So Zero ints never do exact arithmetic JS numbers can't, whether an operand is a literal, a computed value, or an exact int read from storage or input. Compiled `JSON.parse` (`jsonParse`) uses `decodeJson(string)`: integers past ±2^53 decode as the double a JS parser would produce. Stored values, ids and request bodies stay exact (identity and storage keys must not round): compiled code that passes such a value on unchanged (a lookup, a write, a return) passes the exact int; only the arithmetic it does sees the JS number. Comparisons (`<`, `===`) and `String(n)` of an untouched exact int past 2^53 still see the exact value, unlike JS; ids that large only come from storage, where the exact value is the right one.
- `Seam` owns conversions between compiled handles and schema-shaped runtime arrays: Db inputs/results, callback contexts, validators, generators, action/job inputs, Sync envelopes and ability inputs/outputs. User `json()` leaves remain handles in runtime rows. Write inputs detach them from compiled locals; each callback receives a fresh graph. Validator `value` aliases its full path in `ctx.data`; a before-hook's `data`/`patch` aliases `ctx.data` and is read back when no replacement is returned. Native `Extensions` callbacks keep array contracts. A string in a schema callback slot names compiled code; native callbacks use non-string callables.
- Objects enumerate canonical array-index keys in ascending order, then other keys in insertion order (`ownKeys`). Empty objects encode as `{}` and empty arrays as `[]`, including nested JSON and numeric-keyed objects.
- Arrays are dense: `get` returns null for an invalid/missing index; `setAt` permits overwrite or append at length and throws `RangeError` otherwise. Fixed-length walks throw if they reach an index removed by their callback; live-length `from` and `for…of` allow shrinking and growing.
- `get`/`prop` and `setAt`/`set` throw catchable JS `TypeError` for a missing receiver. Writes evaluate their value first; read-modify-write operations read first.
- `has` snapshots property presence for arithmetic compounds and updates. `plus` implements `+=` primitive coercion with that snapshot, distinguishing a missing old value from present null.
- `parseInt(string $s, int|float|null $radix = null): int|float`, `parseFloat(string $s): int|float` — exact JS semantics, NAN when nothing parses.
- `truthy(mixed $v): bool` — null, false, 0, -0.0, NAN, `""` are falsy; every handle (even empty) is truthy.
- `typeOf(mixed $v): string` — `"object"` for null/handles, `"number"`, `"string"`, `"boolean"`, `"function"` for Closure.
- `strictEq(mixed $a, mixed $b): bool` — `===` for primitives: int/float compare numerically, NAN never equal; handles compare by identity.
- `isInteger(mixed $v): bool`, `isFinite(mixed $v): bool` (`Number.isInteger/isFinite`, no coercion).
- `toFixed(int|float $n, int $digits = 0): string` — JS `toFixed`.

Strings (indexes and lengths count UTF-16 code units like JS, so 🙂 is two; negative/float/out-of-range arguments handled exactly like JS):
- `slice(string $s, int|float $start = 0, int|float|null $end = null): string`
- `substring(string $s, int|float $start, int|float|null $end = null): string`
- `charAt(string $s, int|float $i): string`, `strAt(string $s, mixed $i = 0): ?string`

## TypeScript type normalization

Zero uses OXC 0.152.0 to parse TypeScript and keeps its annotations and source
locations in the typed IR. The native and browser/WASM compilers run the same
normalizer before PHP emission. These are type operations, not a JavaScript
engine or a replacement for TypeScript's complete checker. Check authoring
code with strict TypeScript as well as `zero check`.

| Surface | Support | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Interfaces | Supported for finite objects | Multiple `extends` bases, imported named types, generic arguments and inherited optional fields. Reachable merged declarations are refused. Class references use the separate nominal class dispatch described below; finite object operations do not model class prototype keys. |
| Class/type interoperability | Supported within the existing class subset | Local/imported class references retain identity through concrete aliases and object wrappers. Class fields, constructor parameter properties and method signatures can use the finite type operations in this table. PHP compilation normalizes annotation-only `undefined`/`void` to null at every runtime boundary, including reentrant class compilation. This does not add generic classes or class-prototype type introspection. |
| Intersections | Partial | Named finite objects merge recursively; compatible scalar/literal intersections narrow. Optional properties include implicit `undefined` in overlapping value domains under strict TypeScript without `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`; required presence does not remove that value. Conflicting optional domains still allow absence. Impossible object intersections and function/array intersections are refused. |
| Generic aliases/interfaces | Supported for concrete instantiations | Required arguments, scalar/array/finite-object structural constraints, defaults that reference earlier parameters, and nested applications. Constraint checks do not use PHP runtime conversions such as Date-to-number. Missing/extra arguments fail. PHP-reachable generic functions are refused, rather than compiling a signature widened to `unknown`. |
| `keyof` | Supported for finite objects | Literal string keys; object unions retain only common keys. Open maps, arrays, primitive/prototype keys, numeric property names and symbols are refused. |
| Indexed access types | Partial | String-key unions on finite objects, arrays (`T[]`, `Array<T>`, `ReadonlyArray<T>`) with `[number]`, tuple numeric literals/unions and tuple `[number]`. A key missing from any union member fails. Optional reads include `undefined` during normalization and become nullable at the PHP boundary. |
| Dynamic property reads | Supported for finite string keys | `object[key]` works when every possible key belongs to the fixed object. Arbitrary string keys need `Record<string, T>`. This does not add dynamic writes to fixed objects. |
| `Record<K, V>` | Partial | Finite string unions produce required fixed properties; `string` produces the existing open map. Numeric/symbol keys are refused. |
| `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly` | Partial | Finite objects and unions of finite objects. `Required` removes optional presence and its `undefined`, retaining explicit `null`. Readonly is type-only; PHP handles retain their existing identity/mutation semantics. Open-map and array utility transforms are refused. |
| `Pick`, `Omit` | Partial | Finite objects and finite string key unions; object unions use their common keys, with combined value types and presence. `Pick` validates every key. They do not distribute across object unions. |
| `NonNullable` | Partial | Concrete types; removes both `null` and `undefined` before PHP normalization. `unknown` and `void` are refused. |
| `Extract`, `Exclude`, conditional types | Partial | Concrete scalar, array/tuple and finite object comparisons, including structural object matching. Direct naked bound parameters distribute over unions (including boolean); tuple-wrapped checks do not. Check positions must be direct parameters, scalars or object/array/tuple wrappers; aliases and other type operations in check position need an explicit tuple wrapper, because they can change distributivity before instantiation. `null` and `undefined` remain distinct until the PHP boundary. `infer`, unresolved `unknown`, `void`, function/runtime predicates and boxed primitive/array property matching are refused. |
| Mapped types | Partial | Finite string key domains; optional modifiers and homomorphic identity mappings preserve presence. `-?` requires a homomorphic identity mapping. Homomorphic mappings need one finite object; key parameters constrained by a direct `keyof T` preserve presence too. Fresh key sets use literal unions (optionally including `never`), or direct parameters constrained by `string` or literal unions. Aliased or reduced key expressions and constraints, such as `Keys<T>`, `Identity<K>`, `keyof T \| never` and `K \| never`, are refused: their reductions can hide optional presence. Rewrite them as direct `keyof T` or a direct key parameter constrained by `keyof T`. Key remapping, template literal expansion, symbols and open maps are refused. |
| `ReturnType`, `Parameters` | Partial | Concrete function type annotations with required parameters. Generic, optional/rest parameter and overloaded function type transforms are refused. General `typeof` queries remain limited to the existing schema inference operations. |
| `Awaited` | Partial | Nested `Promise` wrappers ending in concrete scalar/array values. Thenable-object, union and `unknown` normalization are refused. |
| Modules | Existing subset | Direct named type imports from relative TS modules, with arguments resolved in the caller's module and bodies/defaults in the declaration's module. No new npm, namespace-import, type re-export/barrel or module-augmentation support. |

Normalization is bounded: 96 nested annotation levels, 16,384 resolution steps
per root annotation (including independent roots reached during class
compilation), and 512 keys per finite key operation. Intersection distribution
checks a maximum of 512 candidate alternatives before expansion; this conservative
limit applies before incompatible or duplicate alternatives are removed. Its
recursive calls, copied type nodes and object-property merges also consume the root resolution
budget. Recursive types produce a located diagnostic. Unsupported types are not replaced with
`unknown` or an unrestricted string key.

JSON `$type` annotations retain the authored domain through `InferSelectModel`
and `InferInsertModel`, including nested JSON columns. Authored model expansion
retains finite enums/locales, finite translation maps, structured write presence,
and distinct fresh-row/translation insert alternatives. Runtime insert
approximations remain separate; query rows retain their finite schema domains.
Their dependencies resolve
independently of registry order. Recursive model dependencies and chains exceeding
96 JSON annotations receive located refusals. Copying inferred model fields and
cached JSON types also consumes the root's 16,384-step work budget, before cloning.
PHP compilation and public client
types apply null normalization after model expansion; generated backend query
types retain the authored domain.

Zero PHP runtime contract

The Rust compiler (zero build) emits WordPress plugins. Everything that runs at request time is PHP: a hand-written runtime library (runtime/Zero/*.php, copied verbatim into every build) plus generated files. This document is the seam between them. The compiler only emits calls listed here.

Requirements (Platform::problems() is the one statement of them; activation and zero doctor both apply it): WordPress 7.1+ on PHP 8.2+ with the mbstring, json and gd extensions (sodium for the identity bundle); MySQL 8.0+ or MariaDB 10.11+ with every Zero table InnoDB, or SQLite through SQLite Database Integration 3.1.2+; the pinned platform plugins Secure Custom Fields, Action Scheduler and MCP Adapter at the versions in Platform::PLUGINS, plus Polylang when the app is localized. Composer runs only at maintainer time; prefixed third-party libraries ship under vendor-prefixed/. See dependencies.md for their locks and regeneration. Every Zero file starts with declare(strict_types=1);. Namespace Zero.

A string in a schema callback slot names compiled code. Seam converts its schema-shaped input and context to JsObject / JsArray handles. Each callback receives a fresh graph; before-hooks’ $data / $patch shares identity with $ctx->p['data'], so in-place mutations are retained without a replacement return. After-hook and delete-hook return values are ignored. Native non-string callables retain PHP array inputs and contexts; before-hooks replace data or patches only when their return is a native array.

Compiled object and array parameters pass handles by value: member mutations are shared, but rebinding a parameter does not replace the caller’s binding. Captured bindings retain that JavaScript behavior, including arrays, open records and optional fields. Object spread/rest copies field values shallowly. Loop-local declarations receive a fresh binding on each execution, and a captured for (let …) header variable receives a fresh Js::cell per iteration. The cell copies its value; copying a handle preserves the referenced container.

Arrays remain dense. Indexed writes may replace an existing element or append at the current length; writes past the end throw a catchable RangeError. Writing through a missing receiver throws TypeError. Assignments evaluate the receiver and key before the value; read-modify-write operations read the old value before evaluating the right-hand side. These are runtime semantics, not a blanket refusal of writes into array elements.

Compiled classes

Generated class methods are plain ZeroApp functions with an explicit first receiver argument. They use JsObject handles for instances, so aliases, closures, member mutations and strict identity use the existing object model. JsObject::$class is readonly descriptor metadata; only JsObject::$p contains enumerable own fields. PHP inheritance and PHP method binding are not used.

JsClass descriptors contain the parent, constructor and ordered field initializer closures, instance/static method tables, and a static JsObject. Generated descriptor factory functions cache one descriptor per class per process. The compiler emits these runtime operations:

  • construct(...$args): JsObject allocates a fresh handle and initializes it.
  • initialize(JsObject $instance, array $args): void runs a constructor on the existing receiver. Base fields precede constructor defaults; generated derived constructors call the parent’s initializer, then their own field initializer.
  • invoke($receiver, $name, $args, $static): mixed selects the actual receiver’s descriptor. invokeOn(...) starts at the lexical parent for super calls while retaining that receiver. Methods receive the hidden receiver explicitly.
  • get, has and set implement static field inheritance. Reads search parents; writes create an own field on the actual class descriptor.
  • isInstance($value, $expected): bool walks descriptor ancestry, never field shapes. Plain/cloned/deserialized objects do not acquire class identity.

Js::prop, has and set also accept descriptors for compiled static field updates. Spread, object keys and JSON visit own properties only. Js::clone and Seam detachment copy the own-field graph into plain handles; descriptors and method tables are not traversed or serialized. Generated client types erase instance identity recursively at the wire boundary.

Write pipeline (Db::insert/update/delete, REST and CLI all go through it)

Viewer-bound writes must not answer existence questions about unreadable data. Setting a non-null unique value (including an explicit primary key or a generated slug) requires an unfiltered collection read rule and visibility of that field across rows. Otherwise both taken and free values return 401/403 before any uniqueness lookup. A filtered read, including self or automatic draft filtering, does not authorize new or changed unique values. An unchanged value is accepted only when the viewer can read the current row and the column cannot hide values. That value is omitted from persistence, and native slug repair preserves it without querying competitors. Publishing a WordPress draft is a new uniqueness operation; echoing or omitting its slug cannot bypass the full visibility preflight. Hidden columns and unreadable rows receive the same refusal before equality can affect the response. Trusted CLI/hook writes retain normal uniqueness checks; successful public creates retain their ordinary row response. System uids remain unguessable sync identities.

Blind intake belongs in a narrow application action, not a public unique-create endpoint. The site example acknowledges newsletter requests with a constant response and queues private, deduplicated processing; it returns neither a subscriber row nor a job identifier. Existing and new subscriptions have the same acknowledgement. Exact announcement recipient counts are admin-only, including filtering: comparing counts around a signup would otherwise disclose membership. Member administrators explicitly have collection read access before managing unique identities. Its editor-only removal action authorizes detaching private subscription links and returns only the post id; private subscriber data never leaves that action. These application policies do not exempt viewer-bound CRUD from the checks above.

Every reference in a viewer-bound write, including generated values, must resolve within the target’s read filters and use a readable target column; an unreadable target and a missing target return the same reference_violation, without the resolved value in its detail. Knowing a sync UID grants no target visibility: primary and non-primary references both require a viewer-scoped lookup, and the write pipeline checks visibility again after hooks. Hidden and absent translation peers both remain unlinked until a visible peer is available. This applies to core WordPress saves too. Sync checks target visibility before resolved values reach input rules or validators. Potential generated constraints are preflighted before defaults and on-update generators run; hook-written references are checked before field validation. A delete requires visibility across the referencing collection and column before checking for children, so hidden children cannot be discovered by trying to delete their parent. The preflight follows cascade branches and covers generated values from referential updates even when a branch has no rows. Hidden cascade branches are refused before traversal, so recursion limits cannot reveal their depth. These checks roll back the whole write on refusal. Changing a referenced key uses the same relationship visibility preflight, following native cascading updates before the database can expose hidden children. Native WordPress draft publication preflights slug visibility before collision resolution. Wrapped saves and editor forms preserve an omitted slug on an already published, scheduled, or private row. Programmatic native writes without known input provenance retain collision resolution and require slug visibility.

Create, per row:

  1. Let registered input normalizers consume virtual inputs, then reject unknown keys (invalid_input, pointer /<key>). The original supplied input remains available to write hooks.
  2. Apply defaults for absent keys: value, now (current UTC timestamp, or today’s date for date), fn. 2b. A required column (notNull, no default, not autoIncrement) that is absent and not listed in the collection’s beforeCreateFills → invalid_input pointer /<col>. Hooks never see a missing required field.
  3. beforeCreate.
  4. Validate + coerce every column (below). Missing required (notNull, no default, not autoIncrement) → invalid_input pointer /<col>.
  5. INSERT. UNIQUE violation → 409 unique_violation with pointer /<col> when the column can be determined. FK violation → 409 reference_violation.
  6. Re-read the row by primary key → afterCreate($row).

Update, per matching row (rows are selected first, then updated by PK):

  1. Normalize virtual input, then reject unknown keys and changing the primary key.
  2. For columns with onUpdate that are absent from the patch, set them.
  3. beforeUpdate($patch, $existing).
  4. Validate + coerce patched columns.
  5. UPDATE by PK; re-read → afterUpdate($row, $previous).

Writes made by hooks or actions through Db run the same pipeline (including hooks). Nesting deeper than 8 levels → HttpError(500, 'hook_recursion', ...).

Every HTTP request and every CLI command runs in one transaction (START TRANSACTION, REPEATABLE READ). An exception before the commit rolls back every write of the request. Two things are outside that guarantee: an afterCommit callback runs after the commit, so its failure propagates without undoing the request; and wp zero migrate records each DDL statement as it succeeds (MySQL DDL commits implicitly), so a later statement’s failure leaves the earlier ones applied and recorded (see Migrations). Transactions run concurrently, so a read whose result the transaction then depends on takes an explicit lock (FOR UPDATE, LOCK IN SHARE MODE; see Sync\Lock, Locale\Lock, Jobs\Storage).

Runtime extension points (schema v3)

Features owns the ordered module list; bootstrap registers it once. A module registers callbacks through Extensions, plus idempotent dialect-specific DDL through SystemTables when needed. Registration itself performs no app I/O.

  • beforeRead(collection, &opts, ?viewer, pointer) runs before query validation and SQL; its normalized options also govern projection at every relation level. Constraint preflights treat extension narrowing as filtered visibility: unique namespaces, generated references, and incoming relationships must remain fully readable before storage can answer about competitors or children. Unchanged unique values must also survive a viewer-scoped read of the current row. Custom beforeRead and onRead callbacks conservatively disable viewer-bound namespace checks, since an arbitrary callback can hide values conditionally. A registration may set constraintSafe: true only when its visibility policy preserves row membership and constraint columns except for restrictions already represented by schema access rules; built-in transforms do so. Concrete references still require a row and matching column value in the final viewer-visible result, including read transforms. Trusted writes remain available. onLookup(collection, pks) runs in concrete stores before hydration and decode. Lookup receives nonempty collection pages, not system-media rows. Mutation results (including receipt replay) and revision snapshots also prime their page before read transforms; callbacks may run again after write hooks.
  • onRead(rows, collection, ?viewer) transforms decoded rows before with and projection; also applies to revision reads and returning write responses. Revision restore authorizes first, then uses the full stored snapshot; display transforms never supply persistence input. Internal mutation selection keeps authorization filters and passes full decoded storage rows to normalization, validation and write hooks, including previous-row notifications. Keep primary keys intact. Relation attachment preserves original linkage privately; removing a media column prevents its population.
  • normalizeWrite(op, collection, &data, ?existing, ?viewer, provided) consumes virtual inputs before column rejection on create/update. Keep it free of persisted effects; unconsumed unknown keys remain errors.
  • onWrite(op, collection, &data, ?existing, ?viewer, provided) runs after defaults/onUpdate and before app before-hooks (create: also before required and access checks). provided is the original row/patch. Delete runs before beforeDelete. onWritten(op, collection, row, ?previous) runs after app after-hooks in the same transaction, including WP editor notifications. WP editor captures use editorRow(collection, pk) to keep full stored values for previous/deleted rows, even when trusted reads have display transforms.
  • afterCommit(fn) delegates to the active Db’s Store. The outermost commit drains its queue; rollback discards it. Outside a transaction it runs immediately. Nested transactions join without savepoints. A callback that throws propagates after commit, without rollback cleanup or callback replay.
  • route(prefix, handler) receives (method, fullDecodedSegments, query, rawBody, viewer, files, form) and returns [status, data] or Response. One complete first segment is matched before built-ins and collections. Thus the auth feature can replace /auth/token; without a registered owner the phase-1 login remains. A module that owns a prefix owns all its dispatch and method checks.
  • beforeAction(spec, name, rawBody, headers, ?viewer) sees exact input bytes and lowercase header names after action authorization, before input validation. JSON syntax parsing retains its phase-1 precedence before action lookup. HTTP and CLI actions share this path; a null viewer means trusted CLI.

Action authorization, raw-body guards and input validation, or create input normalization/required/access checks, run before wrappers, including on replay. Calling next() executes the handler/write pipeline. A wrapper may instead return its stored result and add metadata with Response::withHeaders. Wrapper failures roll back both writes and receipt effects. Create wrappers see the full persisted row; read transforms apply after execution or replay. Db::insert exposes its optional per-row around(callable(): array): array continuation to the request adapter. Trusted nested writes do not inherit the request header or create another receipt.
  • HTTP list and item reads forward feature query options to beforeRead. The feature consumes/normalizes its options; unknown remaining options fail normal query validation.
  • cli(command, handler) receives (argsWithoutCommand, flags) inside the canonical wp zero transaction and receipts.
  • schemaDescribe(fn) transforms the public schema description.

Wp\Migrator applies the app plugin’s zero/app/migrations/NNNN_<name>.sql files (MySQL dialect, {prefix} replaced by $wpdb->prefix) in filename order. class Js — JavaScript semantics in PHP

Static methods on final class Js. Value model: JS number = PHP int|float; string = PHP string (UTF-8; indexes count UTF-16 code units; splitting a surrogate pair throws RangeError); boolean = bool; null and undefined are both PHP null; arrays are Zero\JsArray, plain objects are Zero\JsObject, both handles with identity; class instances are JsObject handles with a non-enumerable JsClass descriptor; functions are Closure; Date values are numbers (epoch ms); RegExp is Zero\RegExp. The compiler emits native PHP whenever types make it safe; these helpers cover the cases where JS and PHP genuinely differ. Each must match the JavaScript result exactly on the inputs its types allow.

Configuration evaluation uses the same UTF-16 units for numeric string indexes, slice and split(""); a result containing a lone surrogate is rejected with a located build diagnostic. split applies its limit before converting units.

String lastIndexOf accepts only literal number/null/undefined positions; a runtime position can hide the erased null/undefined distinction behind an alias, assertion or call. Omit the position or use a literal instead.

Conversions:

  • str(mixed $v): string — String(v). null → "null", bools → "true"/"false", numbers → numStr, list → elements str’d joined by , with null as "", assoc → "[object Object]", RegExp → /src/flags.
  • numStr(int|float $n): string — Number.prototype.toString(): NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, -0 → "0", integral values below 1e21 without exponent, shortest round-trip digits, exponent form 1e+21, 1.5e-7 exactly where JS uses it (≥ 1e21 or < 1e-6).
  • toNumber(mixed $v): int|float — Number(v): null → 0, bool → 0/1, string trimmed of JS whitespace: "" → 0, decimal, 0x/0o/0b prefixes, Infinity/-Infinity, otherwise NAN. Safe integers (|n| ≤ 2^53) return int, larger values float.
  • n(int|float $r): int|float — an int as a JS number: beyond ±2^53 it becomes the nearest double. Compiled a + b, a - b, a * b and unary -a on numbers are add/sub/mul/neg, which take each operand through n() and then the result; ++/-- are preStep/postStep(&$x, ±1) (the place is evaluated once), and **/Math.pow are pow(a, b). So Zero ints never do exact arithmetic JS numbers can’t, whether an operand is a literal, a computed value, or an exact int read from storage or input. Compiled JSON.parse (jsonParse) uses decodeJson(string): integers past ±2^53 decode as the double a JS parser would produce. Stored values, ids and request bodies stay exact (identity and storage keys must not round): compiled code that passes such a value on unchanged (a lookup, a write, a return) passes the exact int; only the arithmetic it does sees the JS number. Comparisons (<, ===) and String(n) of an untouched exact int past 2^53 still see the exact value, unlike JS; ids that large only come from storage, where the exact value is the right one.
  • Seam owns conversions between compiled handles and schema-shaped runtime arrays: Db inputs/results, callback contexts, validators, generators, action/job inputs, Sync envelopes and ability inputs/outputs. User json() leaves remain handles in runtime rows. Write inputs detach them from compiled locals; each callback receives a fresh graph. Validator value aliases its full path in ctx.data; a before-hook’s data/patch aliases ctx.data and is read back when no replacement is returned. Native Extensions callbacks keep array contracts. A string in a schema callback slot names compiled code; native callbacks use non-string callables.

Zero uses OXC 0.152.0 to parse TypeScript and keeps its annotations and source locations in the typed IR. The native and browser/WASM compilers run the same normalizer before PHP emission. These are type operations, not a JavaScript engine or a replacement for TypeScript’s complete checker. Check authoring code with strict TypeScript as well as zero check.

# Upload storage

`uploads` selects one durable backend for the app's private files and standard
WordPress media. Configure it on the server in `defineConfig`; browser clients
keep using `client.files.<resource>` and `client.media`. `file()` and `media()`
references work in both collections and SQL tables, with the same access rules.
The logical file resource and physical provider bucket are different concepts.

```ts
import { defineConfig, env } from "zero";

export default defineConfig({
  name: "catalog",
  uploads: {
    backend: "s3",
    bucket: env("UPLOAD_BUCKET"),
    region: "us-east-1",
    // For Garage, R2, MinIO and other compatible services:
    // endpoint: env("UPLOAD_ENDPOINT"), pathStyle: true,
    prefix: "catalog",
    credentials: {
      accessKeyId: env("UPLOAD_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
      secretAccessKey: env("UPLOAD_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
      // sessionToken: env("UPLOAD_SESSION_TOKEN"),
    },
  },
});
```

Bucket, endpoint, region and prefix accept strings or `env()` references;
credentials require `env()`. Provision the bucket separately, keep public access
blocked, and grant the runtime GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject and
ListBucket within its prefix. TLS verification remains enabled. Set credentials
in each replica's process environment or WordPress configuration constants.
Their values never enter generated clients, schema descriptions or provider
error messages. All replicas must share the database and provider configuration.

The transport uses MIT-licensed AsyncAWS S3 3.5.0, scoped as `Zero\Vendor` and
pinned with its dependencies in the runtime Composer lock. `scripts/vendor.sh
runtime` reproduces the committed bundle and licenses. No signer is implemented
in Zero. S3 reads/uploads stream with bounded memory and finite HTTP deadlines;
image processing still needs PHP's normal memory and temporary disk budget.

## Installation, activation and readiness

The provider adapter ships inside `zero-runtime`; no offload plugin, Composer run
or credentials are needed at build time. As with [plugin dependencies](wp-plugins.md),
installing the generated artifact does not activate it. Deploy and activate the
manifest's dependencies, runtime and app in dependency order. Runtime registration
installs the site's namespace once and schedules one recurring cleanup action;
repeated requests/activation preserve that namespace, unrelated plugin options and
existing media. The adapter does not configure or activate another offload plugin.
Do not run competing upload-directory or attachment-offload integrations together.

Activation is not provider readiness. The deployment owner still provisions the
bucket and least-privilege grant, injects environment values on every replica,
and runs Action Scheduler reliably. Zero does not create cloud accounts, buckets,
IAM policies or migrate existing disk uploads. Before routing traffic, upload and
read a private file and image, generate a size on another replica, then delete
them. A successful build, plugin activation or schema response alone proves none
of those provider permissions. Configured S3 errors fail closed at the operation.

The disposable [WordPress acceptance lane](../tests/wp/README.md) performs actual
provider setup: it initializes a pinned Garage node, creates its isolated bucket,
imports a dedicated test key and grants access. It repeats setup after objects
exist, then proves read/write/list/delete and image processing across replicas.
This is test provisioning, not a production cloud provisioning command.

## Dependency choice

The reviewed alternatives are existing PHP implementations; no JavaScript S3 or
WordPress offload implementation is translated or copied. The adapter calls
AsyncAWS's `S3Client::putObject`, `getObject`, `deleteObject` and `listObjectsV2`;
the SDK owns signing, HTTP and XML. It leaves file identity, grants, transactions
and durable cleanup with Zero's existing database owners. The exact SDK source is
[`43b1f00d16f2c5c05b37337ccdc2aa1b1a24a18a`](https://github.com/async-aws/s3/tree/43b1f00d16f2c5c05b37337ccdc2aa1b1a24a18a),
version 3.5.0 (MIT); Composer locks its transitives and scoped vendoring retains
licenses. See [dependency reproduction](dependencies.md).

Two maintained WordPress alternatives were inspected at fixed releases:

  (GPL-2.0-or-later) provides an S3 stream wrapper, remote image editors and an
  existing-media migration CLI. `S3_UPLOADS_OBJECT_ACL` and
  `s3_uploads_is_attachment_private` support private objects;
  `s3_uploads_s3_client_params` can configure a compatible endpoint. Its
  `Plugin::add_s3_signed_params_to_attachment_url` issues expiring provider URLs

  rollback and after-commit deletion. Its attachment hooks also do not represent

- [WP Offload Media Lite 3.4.4](https://plugins.svn.wordpress.org/amazon-s3-and-cloudfront/tags/3.4.4/)
  (GPLv2) has attachment upload/download/remove handlers, supports local-file

  `as3cf_upload_object_key_as_private`. `AS3CF_SETTINGS` can supply runtime
  settings; `as3cf_aws_s3_client_args` can customize the SDK. Its item/offloaded-file

Both are useful attachment-offload products. Neither is adopted as a second
owner of Zero's upload state in this unit. The smaller SDK transport is the chosen
reuse boundary. These are source/API assessments, not claims that the alternative
plugins passed this project's replica acceptance test. No plugin settings or
existing provider media are overwritten to make the chosen adapter work.

## Serving and processing

Private files retain their existing MIME/size limits, uploader ownership and
five-minute signed API grants. S3 objects have opaque keys under a random site
namespace and hashed app identity. File rows remain in `zero__files`; attachment
manifests remain in WordPress postmeta. Metadata never depends on a replica's disk.

Media remains publicly readable, matching the existing media API. Its originals,
WordPress intermediate sizes, Zero focal crops, scaled originals and image-edit
backups live in the same backend. Stable API URLs serve those bytes through PHP,
with safe MIME/disposition headers. They can be saved in Gutenberg content without
expiring. They are not public S3 URLs. WordPress responsive-image URLs use the same
manifest, and a deleted/replaced variant stops resolving through the API.

Each request uses a private random directory under the system temporary directory
for upload validation and image processing. The standard WordPress upload,
sideload and attachment metadata hooks offload originals and derivatives before
successful return. Image editing hydrates originals and supporting variants into
that scratch directory. Shutdown removes it, so successful work needs no persistent
uploads volume and another replica can continue immediately.

This covers Zero uploads and WordPress attachment uploads through the standard
core/editor/REST APIs, image generation and image edit/restore. A plugin that writes
directly to disk, bypasses attachment hooks, stores a filesystem pathname as its
own durable record, or replaces upload/image hooks must integrate explicitly.
Unattached arbitrary filesystem uploads, plugin caches, themes and plugin installs
are outside this upload contract. This is not an interception layer for every PHP
filesystem write. Disable external image-CDN plugins when using this backend;
they own separate rewrite/offload contracts.

## Failures and recovery

S3 configuration never falls back to durable local bytes. A failed upload returns
an error. Zero's request transaction rolls back metadata, and new objects have
rollback compensation. Replacements use immutable object keys, so rollback keeps
the previous committed version. Deletions revoke database-backed download URLs at
commit and try provider deletion afterwards. Failed deletes do not resurrect rows.
Deletion and rollback compensation check live database references before removing
bytes, so a temporary metadata transition cannot delete a final manifest's objects.
Retirement also invalidates request-local reuse of those objects.
Provider details and signed requests are excluded from public errors and logs.

A DB-backed Action Scheduler action reconciles one page of at most 100 objects
against live file rows and attachment manifests. It only collects unreferenced
objects older than 24 hours, covering process crashes, rollback cleanup failure
and provider outages during deletion. Database/provider read errors fail the action;
they are never interpreted as an empty reference set. Pagination continues through
scheduled actions; hourly runs retry failures. Run Action Scheduler on a reliable
worker/cron in production. Give each app's requests a deadline below the 24-hour
cleanup grace. Keep the namespace option with database backups. For versioned S3
buckets, provider lifecycle rules must expire noncurrent versions/delete markers.

Core WordPress writes outside Zero's API retain core's own metadata/error lifecycle;
they are not silently wrapped in a new transaction model. Partially completed core
attachment operations can require ordinary WordPress metadata repair. The object
reconciler removes bytes only after their database references disappear.

app, or perform a deliberate migration of local file rows and attachment manifests
before enabling it on an existing site. Reads of unmigrated local resources fail

bytes are not silently deleted. Keep the existing backend until that migration is
verified. Changing the bucket, prefix, app identity or site namespace also requires

and private-file web-server protection probes. Omitted configuration retains that
default. Selecting S3 bypasses local `.htaccess` probes; provider authorization and
